levels.name: Source code
levels.description: Actual implementations: compilers, interpreters, runtimes, standard libraries, grammars, conformance suites. Shows how a language can be implemented; it is not the definition of the language.

levels.name: Primary sources
levels.description: What defines the language independent of any implementation: standards, specifications, reference manuals, proposals, formal semantics and the designers' defining papers.

levels.name: Secondary sources
levels.description: Material that explains or analyses the primary sources: tutorials, books, guides, courses, papers, history, comparison guides.

levels.name: Tertiary sources
levels.description: Collections and summaries of other sources: encyclopedias, wikis, catalogs, comparison tables, curated lists.

languages.name: 05AB1E
languages.summary: Adnan's (Adriandmen) stack-based golfing language with a custom code page; originally in Python, rewritten in Elixir.

level_notes.2: Little secondary literature exists beyond the wiki/encyclopedia entries.

languages.name: 1ML
languages.summary: Research ML dialect by Andreas Rossberg that unifies ML's core and module languages into a single language in which modules are first-class values and types are small-'large' values, given meaning by elaboration into System Fω; it supports a simple form of ML-style type inference.

level_notes.0: The prototype interpreter (rossberg/1ml, OCaml) elaborates 1ML into System Fω and evaluates it.
level_notes.1: Defined by the ICFP 2015 paper and its extended/JFP versions, which contain the full formal elaboration semantics.
level_notes.2: No tutorials beyond the papers' examples.

languages.name: 6502 assembly
languages.summary: Assembly language of the 8-bit MOS Technology 6502 microprocessor (and the 65C02/65816 family) used in the Apple II, Commodore 64, Atari 8-bit, BBC Micro and NES; an accumulator machine with zero-page and indexed addressing modes.

level_notes.1: MOS Technology's 1976 programming manual defines the instruction set and the original assembler syntax; modern assemblers (ca65, ACME, 64tass, DASM) each have their own directive syntax.
level_notes.0: No reference implementation; Visual 6502 simulates the original transistor netlist, and emulator cores (MAME, many others) reimplement it.

resources.title: Visual 6502 — transistor-level simulation of the NMOS 6502
MCS6500 Microcomputer Family Programming Manual (MOS Technology, 1976)
ca65 Users Guide — macro assembler for the 6502 family (syntax, expressions, scopes, macros, structs)

languages.name: A-0 / A-2 / MATH-MATIC
languages.summary: Grace Hopper's UNIVAC compiler line: A-0 (1952) linked numbered subroutines from a library, A-2 was distributed with source to users, and MATH-MATIC (AT-3, 1957) added an algebraic English-like notation.

level_notes.0: No surviving A-0/A-2 implementation is publicly available.
level_notes.1: The MATH-MATIC programming manual (UNIVAC U-1568, 1958) survives as a scan on bitsavers; A-0/A-2 primary documents are not online.

resources.title: Knuth & Trabb Pardo — The Early Development of Programming Languages (STAN-CS-76-562)

languages.summary: Arthur Whitney's APL dialect developed at Morgan Stanley (1988) with an X11 GUI toolkit and dependencies; released as open source and a precursor of K.

level_notes.1: The A+ reference manuals survive only as PDFs inside the source mirror (listed at level 0); aplusdev.org no longer resolves.
level_notes.2: No open secondary literature verified.

languages.name: ABAP
languages.summary: SAP's proprietary business-application language running on the SAP NetWeaver/ABAP application server: statement-oriented COBOL-like syntax extended with ABAP Objects, embedded ABAP SQL, internal tables and constructor expressions.

level_notes.1: Defined only by SAP's ABAP Keyword Documentation. help.sap.com serves it as a JavaScript single-page app that answers 200 for any path, so only the documentation entry points are linked; the SAP-maintained ABAP cheat sheets (level 2) are used for concept deep links.
level_notes.0: The SAP kernel/ABAP VM is closed source. abaplint (an open-source TypeScript parser and static checker) and the abaplint transpiler (ABAP to JavaScript) are the available open implementations.

languages.name: ABNF (RFC 5234)
languages.summary: The IETF's BNF variant for protocol syntax: "/" alternatives, n*m repetition, %x numeric terminal values and ranges, case-insensitive quoted strings and a standard set of core rules. Standardised as Internet Standard 68.

level_notes.0: No reference implementation; bap (used by IETF author tools) is the de facto checker.

languages.name: Abstract State Machines
languages.summary: Gurevich's model of computation (originally 'evolving algebras') in which a state is a first-order structure and a program is a set of guarded function updates fired in parallel; Börger's ASM method uses it for stepwise-refined system specification, executed by tools such as ASMETA (AsmetaL), CoreASM and Microsoft's AsmL.

level_notes.1: No standard: the Lipari Guide (1993) and Gurevich's sequential-ASM thesis paper define the model; concrete languages (AsmetaL, CoreASM, AsmL) are each defined by their tool documentation.
level_notes.0: ASMETA (Java/Xtext, AsmetaL) and CoreASM (Java, extensible interpreter) are the maintained open-source toolsets.

languages.name: ACL2
aliases: A Computational Logic for Applicative Common Lisp
languages.summary: Applicative subset of Common Lisp together with a first-order logic of total recursive functions and an automated induction-and-rewriting theorem prover, successor to the Boyer–Moore prover Nqthm and used for industrial hardware verification.

level_notes.1: The ACL2 documentation (XDOC combined manual) is the reference; acl2.org mirrors refuse automated clients, so the UT Austin copy is linked.
level_notes.0: acl2/acl2 on GitHub; the system is written in ACL2/Common Lisp itself.

languages.name: ACPI Source Language / ACPI Machine Language
languages.summary: ASL is the source language in which firmware describes devices and power-management control methods in ACPI tables (DSDT/SSDT); it compiles to AML, a compact bytecode interpreted by the operating system's ACPI interpreter. ASL combines a declarative object namespace (Device, Name, Package, OperationRegion, Field) with methods containing If/While/Switch, integer arithmetic and mutexes.

level_notes.0: ACPICA (Intel's ACPI Component Architecture) is the reference implementation: the iASL compiler/disassembler and the AML interpreter used by Linux, FreeBSD and others. Windows has its own interpreter.
level_notes.1: Chapters 19 (ASL reference) and 20 (AML specification, with grammar and byte encoding) of the ACPI specification are normative; chapter 5 gives the namespace and control-method model.
level_notes.3: Covered within the Wikipedia ACPI article; OSDev wiki AML pages report blocked.

languages.summary: Behavioral specification language for C programs written in annotation comments (contracts, loop invariants, logic functions, predicates), used by Frama-C's WP and E-ACSL plugins.

level_notes.1: The ACSL reference manual (PDF) is the specification.
level_notes.0: Implemented by Frama-C (OCaml).

languages.name: Act 1 / ABCL (actor languages)
languages.summary: Early actor programming languages: MIT's Act 1 (Lieberman/Hewitt) with futures, serializers and delegation, and Yonezawa's ABCL/1 family of concurrent object-oriented languages with past/now/future message types.

level_notes.0: No public Act 1 implementation survives; ABCL implementations were distributed by the University of Tokyo but are not readily available.
level_notes.1: Defined by MIT AI memos (Act 1) and Yonezawa's ABCL book/papers.

languages.name: ActionScript
languages.summary: ECMAScript dialect used to program Adobe (Macromedia) Flash and AIR. ActionScript 3.0 (2006), based on drafts of ECMAScript Edition 4, added classes, packages, namespaces, optional static typing and E4X, and runs as ABC bytecode on the AVM2 virtual machine.

level_notes.0: Adobe open-sourced the AVM2 (avmplus/Tamarin) VM; the Flex/Royale compiler (Falcon) is Apache-licensed; Ruffle reimplements AVM1/AVM2 in Rust.
level_notes.1: No standard (the ECMAScript 4 effort it tracked was abandoned). Adobe's ActionScript 3.0 Language Reference and 'Learning ActionScript 3.0' are the vendor definition.

languages.name: Actor model
languages.summary: Model of concurrent computation in which actors are the universal primitive: on receiving an asynchronous message an actor can send messages, create actors and choose its behaviour for the next message. Formalised by Clinger and Agha, it underlies Erlang/Elixir processes, Akka, Orleans and Pony.

level_notes.0: A model rather than a language: level 0 lists actor runtimes that implement it as libraries (Akka, CAF) and the Rebeca modelling language; Erlang, Elixir and Pony have their own catalog entries.
level_notes.1: Hewitt, Bishop & Steiger (IJCAI 1973) introduced actors; Agha (1986) and Agha-Mason-Smith-Talcott (1997) give operational semantics.

languages.name: Ada
languages.summary: Strongly typed language commissioned by the US DoD for large, long-lived and safety-critical systems: packages with private types, generics, built-in tasking with protected objects and rendezvous, exceptions, range-constrained subtypes, tagged-type OOP and (since 2012) contracts; standardized as ISO/IEC 8652.

level_notes.1: ISO/IEC 8652:2023 (Ada 2022) is the standard; the identical Ada Reference Manual text is freely published by the ARG on ada-auth.org (linked by section), together with the Annotated ARM and Rationale documents. ada-auth.org rejects browser user agents but answers the link checker.
level_notes.0: GNAT (part of GCC, gcc/ada; links use the gcc-mirror GitHub repository) is the main open-source compiler; the ACATS conformance suite validates implementations.

languages.name: Agda
languages.summary: Dependently typed total functional programming language and proof assistant based on Martin-Löf type theory, with dependent pattern matching, mixfix operators, interactive hole-driven development, and extensions such as cubical type theory and sized types.

level_notes.1: No formal specification; the Agda documentation's language reference and Norell's 2007 thesis describe the language. Agda 2 is a complete redesign of the earlier Agda/Alfa systems.
level_notes.0: The Haskell implementation agda/agda is the definition; the type checker lives under src/full/Agda/TypeChecking, the MAlonzo (GHC) and JS backends under Agda/Compiler.

languages.name: Algebraic effects and handlers
languages.summary: Treatment of computational effects as operations of an algebraic theory (Plotkin and Power) with handlers that give them meaning as generalised exception handlers with access to the continuation (Plotkin and Pretnar 2009). It is realised in Eff, Koka, Effekt and OCaml 5 and subsumes exceptions, state, generators and async.

level_notes.0: Research languages (Eff, Koka, Effekt) and OCaml 5's runtime are the implementations; Eff and Koka have their own entries.

languages.name: ALGOL 60
languages.summary: International algorithmic language defined by a committee report that introduced BNF, block structure with lexical scope, recursion, call-by-name and call-by-value parameters and the reference/publication/hardware language distinction; the ancestor of most later imperative languages.

level_notes.1: Defined by the Report (1960), the Revised Report (1963) and the Modified Report (1976, basis of ISO 1538). Open copies: masswerk.at HTML (the HTML uses upper-case NAME anchors that the link checker cannot see, so only whole-page links are given) and scans at the Computer History Museum's Software Preservation Group.
level_notes.0: Original implementations (Dijkstra/Zonneveld X1, Elliott 803, Burroughs B5000, Whetstone) survive only as listings and emulators; modern implementations include GNU MARST (ALGOL 60 to C) and the Racket algol60 language.

languages.name: ALGOL 68
languages.summary: IFIP WG 2.1's orthogonal successor to ALGOL 60, defined with a two-level van Wijngaarden grammar: everything is an expression, user-defined modes (structural types) and operators, unions, references, flexible rows, coercions, parallel clauses and semaphores. Revived in 2025-26 by the GNU Algol 68 front end in GCC.
standards: Revised Report on the Algorithmic Language Algol 68 (IFIP WG 2.1, 1975)

level_notes.1: The Revised Report (Acta Informatica 5, 1975; IFIP WG 2.1) is normative and freely available. Its formal definition uses a two-level (van Wijngaarden) grammar. Modern GNU extensions (modules, stropping, short-circuit operators) are published as GNU68 working-group drafts on algol68-lang.org.
level_notes.0: GNU Algol 68 (ga68) is a GCC front end (gcc/algol68, runtime libga68); its parser is derived from Algol 68 Genie (a68g, Marcel van der Veer's interpreter). Historic implementations: ALGOL 68-R, ALGOL 68C, ALGOL 68S, CDC ALGOL 68.

languages.name: Alloy
languages.summary: Daniel Jackson's lightweight formal specification language based on first-order relational logic with transitive closure ('everything is a relation'); the Alloy Analyzer finds instances and counterexamples within bounded scopes by translating models to SAT through Kodkod. Alloy 6 (2021) adds mutable signatures/fields and linear temporal logic from Electrum.

level_notes.1: No external standard. The online Alloy Language Reference (alloytools.org/spec.html, derived from Appendix B of Software Abstractions) together with the CUP grammar in the Analyzer repository define the language; Jackson's TOSEM 2002 paper defines the original (Alloy 2) semantics. Alloy 6 temporal extensions are documented on alloytools.org/alloy6.html.
level_notes.0: The Alloy Analyzer (Java, AlloyTools/org.alloytools.alloy) is the reference implementation: JFlex/CUP front end, AST in edu.mit.csail.sdg.ast, translation to the Kodkod relational model finder, which emits SAT problems. Forge (Brown) and Electrum are derived implementations.
level_notes.2: Software Abstractions (MIT Press, 2006/2012) is paywalled; the free online books Formal Software Design with Alloy 6 and Practical Alloy, plus Hillel Wayne's community docs, are linked section by section.

languages.name: Befunge / Funge-98
languages.summary: Two-dimensional stack-based language created by Chris Pressey in 1993 to be hard to compile: the instruction pointer moves across a toroidal grid and programs can rewrite themselves with g/p. Funge-98 generalises it to 1-3 dimensions with unbounded space, a stack of stacks, concurrency and fingerprint extensions.

level_notes.1: Befunge-93 is defined by Pressey's documentation; Funge-98 by the 1998 Final Specification (authored by Pressey with the Befunge mailing list) plus the Cat's Eye fingerprint library. No formal semantics.
level_notes.0: bef.c is the Befunge-93 reference; for Funge-98 cfunge and CCBI are the most conforming implementations, with Mycology as the de-facto conformance suite.
level_notes.2: Little tutorial literature beyond the specs; write-ups and IDEs listed.

languages.name: C
languages.summary: Portable systems programming language created at Bell Labs for Unix; a small, manually memory-managed, statically typed procedural language standardized by ISO/IEC JTC1/SC22/WG14 and the lingua franca of operating systems, runtimes and foreign-function interfaces.

level_notes.0: No reference implementation: GCC and Clang/LLVM are the dominant compilers; TinyCC, chibicc, lcc and cproc are small readable ones; CompCert is a formally verified compiler. The standard library is a separate project (glibc, musl, ...).
level_notes.1: The ISO/IEC 9899 standard is paywalled. The freely available WG14 working drafts are linked instead: N3220 (first draft after C23, practically identical to it), N1570 (C11) and N1256 (C99). Section deep links use the HTML rendering of N3220 hosted at port70.net, whose anchors are the standard's clause numbers.
level_notes.2: cppreference.com (a community-maintained reference that paraphrases the standard) is treated as level 2; it answers 403 to automated clients, so those links are reported as 'blocked' by the checker.
level_notes.3: Wikipedia has separate articles for syntax, data types, the standard library and each standard revision.

languages.name: CakeML

level_notes.1: The language is defined by the HOL4 scripts in semantics/ (lexer, grammar, abstract syntax, functional big-step semantics, type system); these are listed at level 1 as formal semantics.

languages.name: CBOR

languages.name: Combinatory logic (SKI)
languages.summary: A variable-free notation for computation using only application and a few primitive combinators (S and K suffice, with I = SKK); equivalent in power to the lambda calculus via bracket abstraction, Turing-complete, and used to compile functional languages (Turner's SKI reduction machines).

level_notes.0: Theoretical model: level 0 lists mechanised CL (HOL4 Church-Rosser for SK), and binary-CL universal machines/programs by Tromp; esoteric languages Unlambda and Lazy K are separate catalog entries.
level_notes.1: Defined by Schönfinkel (1924) and independently by Curry (1930); Curry & Feys (1958) is the classic monograph.

languages.name: Common Lisp
languages.summary: ANSI-standardized Lisp dialect unifying MacLisp descendants, with CLOS multiple dispatch and a metaobject protocol, a restartable condition system, packages, and powerful non-hygienic macros.

languages.name: C++
languages.summary: Multi-paradigm systems language that grew out of C with classes: deterministic destruction (RAII), templates and concepts, zero-overhead abstractions, and an ISO standard revised every three years (C++11 ... C++26). Implemented independently by GCC, Clang and MSVC.

level_notes.0: No reference implementation: the three major independent implementations are GCC (g++ front end in gcc/cp, libstdc++), Clang/LLVM (clang/, libc++, libc++abi) and MSVC (compiler closed, STL open). Source links point at the main/master/trunk branches and can move as the projects refactor.
level_notes.1: The ISO/IEC 14882 standard is paywalled. The working draft is public: eel.is/c++draft is an HTML rendering of the current draft (now the C++26 working draft) with stable [section.name] URLs; timsong-cpp.github.io/cppwp/nNNNN hosts frozen drafts per standard (n4861 = C++20, n4950 = C++23). WG21 papers (Pnnnn/Nnnnn at open-std.org) are the proposal record. The Itanium C++ ABI is a separate, de-facto binary standard.
level_notes.2: isocpp.org and cppreference.com refuse automated clients from the checking sandbox (reported 'blocked'); their URLs are long-standing and were kept.
level_notes.3: cppreference.com is filed under level 3 (community wiki summarising the standard) although practitioners use it as the everyday reference.

languages.name: CPython bytecode
languages.summary: The stack-based bytecode executed by CPython's virtual machine, stored in code objects and cached in .pyc files; an unstable, implementation-specific format that changes every minor release (wordcode since 3.6, adaptive specializing instructions since 3.11).

level_notes.1: No specification: the dis module documentation lists the instructions of the current release only, and PEPs describe interpreter changes. Bytecode is explicitly not a stable interface.
level_notes.0: CPython (Python/bytecodes.c generates the interpreter cases) is the sole definition; other Pythons (PyPy, GraalPy) use different internal formats.
level_notes.3: No dedicated encyclopedia, PLDB or Rosetta entry exists; see the python entry for tertiary sources.

languages.name: C#
languages.summary: Statically typed, garbage-collected object-oriented language for the .NET Common Language Infrastructure, standardised as ECMA-334. Known for properties, delegates and events, reified generics, LINQ query expressions, async/await, value types (structs), pattern matching and nullable reference types.

level_notes.0: Roslyn (dotnet/roslyn) is the compiler; execution is by the .NET runtime (dotnet/runtime: CoreCLR with the RyuJIT compiler and GC, Mono, NativeAOT) whose System.Private.CoreLib implements the built-in types. Mono's older mcs compiler is an independent implementation. Both main repositories are too large to list here, so links target individual files on main.
level_notes.1: ECMA-334 (7th edition, 2023 = C# 7) is the ratified standard; the specification published on learn.microsoft.com is the working draft from dotnet/csharpstandard and is ahead of it. Features newer than the draft are defined by the dotnet/csharplang proposals ('feature specifications'). The run-time semantics rest on ECMA-335 (CLI), which is only published as PDF. The keyword/operator/type pages of the Microsoft C# language reference are filed at level 1 as reference manual.
level_notes.2: Microsoft's 'Tour of C#', 'Fundamentals' and 'Programming guide' material is tutorial/guide content and is filed at level 2.

languages.name: CSS
typing: dynamically checked at parse and computed-value time
languages.summary: Declarative stylesheet language of the web: rules pair selectors (patterns over the document tree) with property declarations, and the cascade, inheritance and per-module layout algorithms turn them into presentation. Defined today as a large family of independently levelled W3C modules rather than one versioned specification.

level_notes.0: No reference implementation. The definition is exercised by the three browser style/layout engines (Blink, Gecko with Servo's Stylo, WebKit), by standalone parsers (rust-cssparser, PostCSS, CSSTree, Lightning CSS, tinycss2), layout libraries (Taffy) and by the shared web-platform-tests suite; the Bikeshed spec sources in w3c/csswg-drafts are listed as tooling. Chromium source is linked on chromium.googlesource.com because the GitHub mirror rate-limits raw fetches.
level_notes.1: There is no single "CSS specification" after CSS 2.1: the language is the set of modules listed in the current CSS Snapshot. Deep links point at the CSSWG editor's drafts (drafts.csswg.org / drafts.css-houdini.org), whose section anchors match the dated W3C TR publications; www.w3.org/TR links are the normative published versions.
level_notes.2: MDN is treated as secondary (explains the specs). Formal-semantics work on CSS layout is academic (Cassius, Meyerovich & Bodik) and listed here rather than at level 1 because it is not part of the definition.
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code has no meaningful CSS category; compatibility tables (caniuse, web-features) play the role of comparison tables.

languages.name: CSV
languages.summary: Plain-text tabular format of records separated by line breaks and fields separated by commas, with double-quote quoting. In use since the early 1970s; RFC 4180 (2005) documented the common form and registered text/csv, and W3C's CSV on the Web added a model and metadata vocabulary. Dialects (delimiters, quoting, encodings, headers) remain the main interoperability problem.
standards: W3C Model for Tabular Data and Metadata on the Web

level_notes.1: RFC 4180 is informational, not a standards-track definition; it documents common practice and registers text/csv. The W3C CSV on the Web recommendations (2015) define a tabular data model, parsing hints and a JSON metadata vocabulary; Frictionless Table Dialect describes dialect parameters.
level_notes.0: No reference implementation; widely used parsers (CPython _csv, Go encoding/csv, rust-csv, libcsv, Papa Parse) define their own dialect options.

languages.name: Datalog
languages.summary: Function-free Horn-clause logic language used as a recursive query language for deductive databases; semantics by least fixpoint/minimal model, with stratified negation and aggregation in modern engines (Soufflé, DDlog, Datomic, Nemo, CozoDB).

level_notes.1: No standard: Datalog is defined in the database-theory literature (Gallaire & Minker 1978; Ceri, Gottlob & Tanca 1989; the Alice book). Engine manuals define concrete dialects.
level_notes.0: Many independent engines with different surface syntax: Soufflé, DDlog, Datafrog, Nemo, Mangle, Racket Datalog, DataScript, Crepe, Ascent, Flix, Formulog, egglog.

languages.name: EDSAC initial orders and order code
languages.summary: Order code of the Cambridge EDSAC (1949), the first practical stored-program computer in regular service, together with David Wheeler's 'initial orders': a bootstrap loader in uniselector ROM that translated mnemonic orders punched on paper tape into binary, making it arguably the first assembler. Initial Orders 2 added relocation and the subroutine library conventions (the 'Wheeler jump').

level_notes.0: No original source exists beyond the published order listings; modern simulators (Campbell-Kelly's Warwick EDSAC simulator, Martin Richards' BCPL interpreter) reproduce Initial Orders 1 and 2.
level_notes.1: Wilkes, Wheeler and Gill, 'The Preparation of Programs for an Electronic Digital Computer' (1951), the first programming textbook, defines the order code, initial orders and subroutine library.
level_notes.3: Wikipedia; Rosetta Code 'EDSAC order code' category reports blocked.

languages.name: Elixir
languages.summary: Dynamic functional language on the Erlang VM (BEAM) with Erlang's actor-style processes and OTP, a macro system based on quoted expressions, protocols for polymorphism, and a gradual set-theoretic type system being added incrementally.

level_notes.0: There is one implementation: elixir-lang/elixir. The bootstrap compiler is written in Erlang (lib/elixir/src: tokenizer, yecc grammar, expander, translation to Erlang abstract format) and the rest of the language (Kernel macros, type checker, standard library, Mix, ExUnit, IEx) in Elixir itself. Execution relies on erlang/otp (BEAM emulator, scheduler, per-process GC), so key OTP files are linked too.
level_notes.1: No formal specification or standard exists; the reference implementation and its versioned documentation on hexdocs.pm (Syntax reference, Operators, Patterns and guards, Typespecs, Kernel.SpecialForms) define the language. Language changes are proposed on the elixir-lang-core mailing list rather than through numbered RFCs. hexdocs.pm/elixir/* currently redirects to elixir.hexdocs.pm/*.

languages.name: Erlang
languages.summary: Dynamically typed functional language from Ericsson built around lightweight isolated processes, asynchronous message passing, links/monitors and supervision ('let it crash'), with hot code loading and transparent distribution. It runs on the BEAM virtual machine and ships with the OTP libraries and design principles.

level_notes.0: Erlang/OTP (erlang/otp) is the reference implementation: the compiler is written in Erlang (lib/compiler, with the scanner/parser/linter in lib/stdlib), the BEAM emulator, JIT (BeamAsm) and runtime in C/C++ under erts/. AtomVM and Firefly are independent BEAM-compatible implementations; HiPE (native compiler) was removed in OTP 24.
level_notes.1: No formal standard. The 'Erlang Reference Manual' in the OTP documentation is the normative description of the current language; changes go through Erlang Enhancement Proposals (EEPs). The 1999 'Erlang 4.7.3 Reference Manual' draft (Barklund & Virding) is the only attempt at a full specification and is long outdated; Core Erlang has its own specification.
level_notes.2: Official user's guides (Getting Started, Programming Examples, Efficiency Guide, OTP Design Principles, Interoperability Tutorial) and the ERTS/compiler internal documentation are listed at level 2.

level_notes.1: The ISO 9074 standard is paywalled and no longer widely distributed; the 1987 Budkowski/Dembinski introduction is the standard reference.
level_notes.0: Historical tools (EDT, Pet/Dingo, Open Estelle) are no longer maintained; an early Estelle-to-C compiler report is linked.

languages.name: Finite automata (DFA/NFA)
languages.summary: Machines with a finite set of states that read input symbols and change state by a transition function (deterministic) or relation (nondeterministic); they recognise exactly the regular languages, with Mealy/Moore variants producing output, and underlie lexers, regex engines, protocols and hardware controllers.

level_notes.0: Theoretical model: level 0 lists automata libraries (Python automata-lib, dk.brics.automaton) and mechanised theory (Coq reglang, Isabelle AFP), plus the JFLAP simulator.
level_notes.1: Defined across McCulloch-Pitts (1943), Kleene (1951/56), Mealy/Moore (1955/56) and Rabin & Scott (1959), which introduced nondeterminism and the subset construction. Kleene's RAND memo reports as blocked from the sandbox.

languages.name: FIRRTL
languages.summary: Intermediate representation for synchronous digital circuits produced by Chisel and other generators; a textual language of circuits, modules, typed ground/aggregate signals, last-connect semantics and conditionals that compilers (the Scala FIRRTL compiler, now CIRCT firtool) lower to Verilog.

level_notes.1: The FIRRTL specification (chipsalliance/firrtl-spec, versioned releases) is normative; the 2016 Berkeley tech report is the original specification.
level_notes.2: Little secondary literature targets FIRRTL directly; tutorials teach it through Chisel (see chisel).
level_notes.0: The original Scala compiler (chipsalliance/firrtl) is deprecated; CIRCT (llvm/circt) firtool is the current implementation.

languages.name: First-order logic
languages.summary: Classical predicate logic with quantifiers over individuals, function and relation symbols and equality; complete (Gödel 1930) but undecidable (Church, Turing 1936). It is the specification language underlying databases (relational calculus), logic programming, SMT and most program logics.

level_notes.1: No single defining document; the classic primary texts (Frege, Hilbert-Ackermann, Gödel, Gentzen, Church) are mostly paywalled or in German. SEP and open textbooks give the standard modern definition.
level_notes.0: Mechanised syntax/semantics (Lean mathlib model theory, Isabelle/FOL, Coq) and automated provers (Vampire, E).

languages.name: ><> (Fish)
languages.summary: Harpyon's 2D stack-based language (2009) where an instruction pointer swims across a grid; supports multiple stacks and self-modification.

level_notes.1: The specification lives on the esolangs.org page; fishlanguage.com (online interpreter) did not respond.

level_notes.2: Little secondary literature exists beyond the wiki/encyclopedia entries.

languages.name: fish (friendly interactive shell)
languages.summary: Interactive shell with a deliberately simple, non-POSIX scripting language: every variable is a list, no word splitting, blocks end with `end`, universal variables shared across sessions, and built-in autosuggestions and completions. Rewritten from C++ to Rust in fish 4.0 (2025).

level_notes.1: No formal specification; "The fish language" chapter of the official documentation describes the implementation.
level_notes.0: fish-shell/fish-shell (Rust since 4.0; earlier releases C++) is the definition.

languages.name: FlatBuffers
languages.summary: Google's zero-copy serialization library and schema language: tables with vtables for optional fields, fixed-layout structs, unions and vectors, readable in place without parsing; flatc compiles .fbs schemas to many languages and can also parse JSON.

level_notes.1: flatbuffers.dev schema and internals pages; reflection.fbs is the schema-of-schemas.
level_notes.0: google/flatbuffers (flatc compiler and runtimes).

languages.name: Flink SQL
languages.summary: Apache Flink's SQL dialect for unified stream and batch processing over dynamic tables, built on Apache Calcite, with time attributes, window table-valued functions and MATCH_RECOGNIZE.

level_notes.2: Little independent tutorial/book literature exists beyond the vendor documentation; vendor guides are listed at level 1.

languages.name: Flix
languages.summary: Functional-first JVM language from Aarhus University and the University of Waterloo combining Hindley-Milner type inference, traits, a polymorphic effect system with algebraic effect handlers and regions, and first-class Datalog constraints (fixpoint computations over lattices).

level_notes.0: The only implementation is the Flix compiler (flix/flix), written in Scala and compiling to JVM bytecode; the standard library is written in Flix.
level_notes.1: No formal specification. The official book 'Programming Flix' (doc.flix.dev) is the reference documentation and is listed at level 1 together with the API docs and the defining research papers (ACM links are reported blocked from the sandbox).

languages.name: Forth

level_notes.0: Gforth is the GNU reference system; pForth, JONESFORTH and zForth are small open implementations; SwiftForth/VFX are commercial.

languages.name: Fortran
languages.summary: The first widely used high-level language (IBM, 1957), still central to numerical and high-performance computing: whole-array operations, modules, derived types with type-bound procedures, pure/elemental procedures, coarrays for SPMD parallelism and standardized C interoperability; ISO/IEC 1539.

level_notes.1: ISO/IEC 1539-1:2023 is paywalled; the J3 committee's final working draft 23-007r1 (Draft Fortran 2023) is freely downloadable and linked with #page= anchors to clauses (page numbers are physical PDF pages).
level_notes.0: gfortran (GCC) and LLVM Flang are the main open-source compilers (Intel ifx, NAG, Cray etc. are proprietary); links use the gcc-mirror and llvm-project GitHub repositories.

languages.name: FP / FL (Backus)
languages.summary: Backus's function-level language from his 1977 Turing Award lecture: programs are built from primitive functions and combining forms without variables, with an algebra of programs. FL (IBM Almaden, 1980s) was its successor with exceptions, I/O and higher-order functions.

level_notes.0: No original IBM FP/FL implementation source is public; level 0 lists third-party FP interpreters and compilers (Valencia, Biagioni). The Berkeley FP manual and the IFP Byte article are listed at level 2.
level_notes.1: Defined by Backus's 1978 paper and the IBM FL language manuals (scanned at the Software Preservation Group).

languages.name: Fauna FQL
languages.summary: Query language of the Fauna distributed document-relational database. FQL v4 was an S-expression-like functional API embedded in host-language drivers; FQL v10 (2023) is a TypeScript-inspired language with method chaining over sets (Collection.where(...).order(...).map(...)), projection, user-defined functions and optional static type checking.

level_notes.1: The vendor reference (docs.fauna.com) is no longer reachable after the Fauna service shut down in 2025; no level-1 document could be linked. The open-sourced server README describes FQL and Fauna Schema Language.
level_notes.0: Fauna open-sourced its database core (fauna/faunadb, Scala): FQL v10 lexer/parser, AST, a type checker with structural/gradual types, and the interpreter and standard library. Official drivers (fauna-js, fauna-go, fauna-dotnet) show the wire protocol and query composition.
level_notes.3: No Wikipedia article for Fauna; PLDB's 'fql' is an unrelated language.

languages.name: Frank

languages.name: F#
languages.summary: Functional-first, strongly typed ML-family language for .NET with type inference, discriminated unions, pattern matching, computation expressions, units of measure and type providers; also compiles to JavaScript via Fable.

level_notes.0: dotnet/fsharp holds the only full compiler (fsc/fsi, FSharp.Compiler.Service) and FSharp.Core. Pipeline: lex.fsl -> LexFilter (offside rule) -> pars.fsy -> SyntaxTree -> Checking (type inference, constraint solving) -> TypedTree -> Optimizer -> IlxGen -> AbstractIL writer. Fable reuses the front end and emits JavaScript and other targets.
level_notes.1: The F# Language Specification (community-maintained at fsharp.github.io/fslang-spec, continuing the F# 4.1 PDF) is the normative text; features added since 4.1 are specified by fslang-design RFCs, and the Microsoft Learn language reference is the official reference manual. No ISO/ECMA standard.

languages.name: GHC Core / STG (as intermediate languages)

languages.name: Haskell
languages.summary: Purely functional, non-strict (lazy) language with Hindley-Milner type inference extended by type classes; defined by the Haskell 2010 Report and, in practice, by GHC and its many language extensions.

level_notes.0: GHC is the de-facto implementation; its pipeline is Lexer.x/Parser.y -> renamer (GHC/Rename) -> type checker (GHC/Tc) -> desugarer (GHC/HsToCore) -> Core optimiser -> STG -> Cmm -> native/LLVM/JS/Wasm back ends, with the runtime system in rts/. The canonical repository is gitlab.haskell.org/ghc/ghc; links use the official github.com/ghc/ghc mirror. Hugs, MicroHs and UHC are independent implementations.
level_notes.1: The Haskell 2010 Language Report is the last committee standard (no ISO/ECMA standard). Modern Haskell is defined by the GHC User's Guide 'Language extensions' chapter and by accepted GHC proposals; System FC (docs/core-spec) is the formal core calculus.
level_notes.2: Real World Haskell (book.realworldhaskell.org) was unreachable from the research sandbox and is therefore not linked.
level_notes.3: The taxonomy has no 'monads' concept; monad material is tagged purity/input-output/statements (do-notation) where that is what the section covers.

languages.name: Hazel
languages.summary: Live functional programming environment and language from the Future of Programming Lab (University of Michigan) organised around typed holes: every editor state is well-typed and runnable because missing or erroneous code is represented by holes, giving total type-error localisation, live evaluation around holes and livelits; it is built on the Hazelnut structure-editor calculus.

level_notes.0: The only implementation is hazelgrove/hazel (OCaml/Reason compiled to JavaScript with js_of_ocaml), which runs in the browser.
level_notes.1: Defined by the Hazelnut family of papers (POPL 2017, ICFP 2019, POPL 2024, ...), which give the formal calculi; there is no user-level language reference.

level_notes.0: Ross Paterson's interpreter (C), with a reference manual and Roger Bailey's tutorial in its doc directory, survives in a GitHub copy (dmbaturin/hope); Paterson's City University page was unreachable during research.
level_notes.1: Defined by the 1980 LISP Conference paper by Burstall, MacQueen and Sannella (open author copy linked) and by the reference manual distributed with the interpreter.

languages.name: Horn clauses
languages.summary: Clauses with at most one positive literal. Their satisfiability is decidable in linear time (propositional case), they have least-model semantics, and with SLD resolution they form the computational core of Prolog and Datalog; constrained Horn clauses are a common intermediate language for program verifiers.

level_notes.0: Logic programming systems (other entries) and constrained-Horn-clause solvers such as Z3/Spacer and Eldarica.

languages.name: HP-GL
languages.summary: Pen-plotter command language from Hewlett-Packard: two-letter mnemonics (IN, SP, PU, PD, PA, PR, CI, LB) with numeric parameters move pens and draw vectors, arcs and labels; HP-GL/2 is embedded in PCL 5 and still read by cutters and CAD tools.

level_notes.1: The HP-GL/2 and HP RTL Reference Guide is out of print; scans circulate unofficially.
level_notes.0: Open readers exist in Ghostscript (GhostPCL) and plotting tools.
level_notes.2: Little open secondary literature.

languages.name: HQL / JPQL
designers: JCP / Eclipse Jakarta EE Persistence expert group
languages.summary: JPQL (Jakarta Persistence Query Language) and its superset HQL (Hibernate Query Language) are SQL-like, object-oriented query languages over entity models: path navigation over associations, fetch joins, polymorphic queries, bulk update/delete, translated to the database's SQL by ORM providers.

level_notes.0: Hibernate ORM's ANTLR 4 grammars and semantic query builder (SQM); EclipseLink is the Jakarta Persistence compatible implementation.
level_notes.1: The Jakarta Persistence specification defines JPQL (with full BNF); the Hibernate Query Language guide defines HQL's extensions.
level_notes.2: Tutorial-style material is mostly embedded in the Hibernate guide (level 1); no separate free secondary source verified.

languages.name: HTML
languages.summary: The markup language of the World Wide Web. Since 2019 the WHATWG HTML Living Standard is the single authoritative definition; it specifies the element vocabulary and content models, the DOM-based data model, and an exact error-tolerant parsing algorithm (tokenizer state machine plus tree-construction insertion modes).

level_notes.0: HTML is defined by a specification, not an implementation, but the parsing chapter is an executable algorithm, so parsers are near-transliterations of it. Listed: html5lib (the first implementation, with the shared html5lib-tests corpus), web-platform-tests (the conformance suite), html5ever, parse5, the Gecko/Blink/WebKit/Ladybird parsers, several library parsers, the Nu Html Checker (RELAX NG schemas for document conformance) and the spec source itself. The html5lib-tests tree-construction files are linked as a directory because raw file fetches of that path fail from the research sandbox.
level_notes.1: The WHATWG HTML Living Standard is normative (W3C ceased publishing a competing HTML in 2019; see the MOU). Section numbers in titles drift as the standard changes; the fragment ids are stable. Historical versions (the 1992 "HTML Tags" note, RFC 1866, HTML 3.2, HTML 4.01, W3C HTML5) are included for history. w3.org answers some automated clients with 403, so those links may show as blocked in the link checker; they were verified manually.
level_notes.2: MDN and web.dev are the main maintained tutorials/references; Simon Pieters' "Idiosyncrasies of the HTML parser" is the standard secondary text on the syntax and parser.

level_notes.2: Secondary literature is mostly blog posts; the huffmate library serves as by-example material.

languages.name: Icon
languages.summary: High-level language from the University of Arizona, successor to SNOBOL4, built around goal-directed evaluation: expressions succeed or fail rather than returning booleans, generators produce sequences of results on backtracking, and string scanning replaces SNOBOL patterns.

level_notes.0: The Arizona implementation (version 9.5, C plus the RTL runtime language) is preserved at github.com/gtownsend/icon; Unicon extends the same code base.
level_notes.1: No standard; 'The Icon Programming Language' (3rd ed., free PDF) and the Icon reference pages are the definition. The Implementation book documents the virtual machine.
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code reports 'blocked' to automated checkers.

languages.name: Id (dataflow)
languages.summary: Implicitly parallel, mostly functional language developed by Arvind's group (UC Irvine, then MIT) for the tagged-token dataflow architecture and the Monsoon machine; non-strict evaluation with I-structures (write-once) and M-structures for controlled side effects, Hindley-Milner typing, and later the basis of pH (parallel Haskell).

level_notes.0: No public source of the Id compiler (Id World / Monsoon) is known; Memo 328 describes its structure.
level_notes.1: The Id Reference Manual (CSG Memo 284, version 90.1) is the definition; Id Nouveau (Memo 265) and the I-structures paper are the defining papers.

languages.name: INI files

languages.name: Java
languages.summary: Statically typed, class-based, garbage-collected language compiled to JVM bytecode. It is defined by two vendor specifications maintained through the Java Community Process and OpenJDK: the Java Language Specification (source language) and the Java Virtual Machine Specification (class files and execution).

level_notes.0: OpenJDK (openjdk/jdk) is the reference implementation: javac lives in src/jdk.compiler, the HotSpot VM in src/hotspot and the class library in src/java.base. Independent implementations include the Eclipse compiler (ECJ), Eclipse OpenJ9 and GraalVM. The TCK (JCK) that decides conformance is not open source; jtreg tests in the OpenJDK tree are the public stand-in.
level_notes.1: No ISO/ECMA standard. The JLS and JVMS (one edition per Java SE release, produced by a JSR) are normative; language changes arrive as JEPs, often first as preview features (JEP 12). The Java SE API specification is the third normative part of a Java SE platform release.
level_notes.2: Oracle's dev.java tutorials supersede the older 'Java Tutorials' (frozen at JDK 8) which are still widely cited.

languages.name: JavaScript
languages.summary: Dynamically typed, prototype-based language with first-class functions, created for Netscape Navigator and standardized as ECMAScript (ECMA-262); it runs in every web browser and in server/embedded runtimes such as Node.js, Deno, Bun and QuickJS.

level_notes.0: There is no reference implementation; ECMA-262 is implemented independently by V8 (Chrome, Node.js), SpiderMonkey (Firefox), JavaScriptCore (Safari), QuickJS, Hermes and others. engine262 mirrors the specification text clause by clause, and test262 is the official conformance suite. SpiderMonkey links use the mozilla-firefox/firefox GitHub repository.
level_notes.1: ECMA-262 is published yearly by Ecma International (also adopted as ISO/IEC 16262); the living draft at tc39.es/ecma262 is the authoritative text between editions. Changes go through the staged TC39 proposal process. Host features (event loop, workers, DOM, Node.js modules) are specified outside ECMA-262.
level_notes.2: MDN is treated as secondary: it is the de-facto reference but is not normative.

languages.name: Jinja
languages.summary: Text template language for Python with Python-like expressions, {% %} control tags, filters, macros and block-based template inheritance; templates are compiled to Python code. Used by Flask, Ansible, dbt, Salt and many static-site and configuration tools, and re-implemented in several other host languages.

level_notes.0: pallets/jinja (Python) is the reference implementation: lexer -> parser -> AST (nodes) -> optional optimizer -> Python source code generator -> runtime. Independent implementations of the same template language exist for Rust (MiniJinja), JavaScript (Nunjucks), Java (Jinjava), C++ (Jinja2Cpp) and Go (pongo2 follows the Django/Jinja syntax).
level_notes.1: There is no formal specification or grammar. The 'Template Designer Documentation' in the official docs is the de-facto language reference, the API and Extensions chapters document the embedding interface, and the reference implementation decides everything else.
level_notes.2: Much of the tutorial literature is written from the viewpoint of a host tool (Flask, Ansible, dbt, Salt, Home Assistant), each of which adds its own filters and globals.
level_notes.3: Encyclopedic coverage is thin; the Wikipedia article and the comparison table of web template engines are the main tertiary sources.

languages.name: JSON Schema
languages.summary: Declarative, JSON-encoded vocabulary for describing, annotating and validating JSON documents; a schema is a set of keyword constraints (assertions, applicators, annotations) applied to an instance, with URI-based identification and referencing of subschemas.

level_notes.0: There is no single reference implementation. The official JSON-Schema-Test-Suite is the de-facto conformance suite and the Bowtie harness reports every implementation's results against it; ajv (JavaScript, compiles schemas to code), python-jsonschema, Hyperjump, santhosh-tekuri/jsonschema (Go), jsonschema-rs and networknt (Java) are widely used independent validators.
level_notes.1: Published as a series of IETF Internet-Drafts that never became RFCs ('draft-04', 'draft-06', 'draft-07', '2019-09', '2020-12'); the dialect meta-schemas are normative companions. Since 2022 the project has decoupled from the IETF process and is preparing a self-published stable release (see the ADRs in json-schema-spec).
level_notes.2: 'Understanding JSON Schema' (hosted on json-schema.org) is the standard book-length guide; learnjsonschema.com documents every keyword of every dialect.

languages.name: JSON
languages.summary: Minimal text format for structured data derived from JavaScript literal syntax: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false and null. Defined twice (RFC 8259 / STD 90 and ECMA-404), deliberately unversioned, and the lingua franca of web APIs and configuration.

level_notes.0: JSON has no reference implementation: json.org's JSON_checker and Crockford's json2.js are historical reference code, and nst/JSONTestSuite is the de-facto conformance corpus. Level 0 therefore samples widely used parsers/serializers in many host languages, with files tagged by the part of the format they implement (lexing, number conversion, string escaping, UTF-8 validation, duplicate keys, depth limits).
level_notes.1: Two co-equal normative texts: RFC 8259 (IETF STD 90; grammar in ABNF plus interoperability guidance) and ECMA-404 (syntax only, railroad diagrams; also published as ISO/IEC 21778). They are intended to describe the same language. ECMA-262's JSON.parse/JSON.stringify, I-JSON (RFC 7493) and JCS (RFC 8785) are linked as normative profiles; JSON Pointer/Patch/Path and JSON Schema have their own catalog entries.
level_notes.2: Much of the secondary literature is about interoperability hazards (numbers, duplicate keys, invalid Unicode) and about parser engineering (SIMD, on-demand parsing).
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code has a JSON task rather than a category.

languages.name: JVM bytecode and class file format
languages.summary: The stack-based instruction set and binary class-file format of the Java Virtual Machine, verified at load time and executed by interpreters and JIT compilers; the compilation target of Java, Kotlin, Scala, Clojure, Groovy and many other languages.
standards: The Java Virtual Machine Specification, Java SE 25 Edition

level_notes.1: The JVMS (one edition per Java SE release) is normative and implementation-independent; JEPs/JSRs record evolution. The verifier's type-checking rules are given in Prolog in JVMS 4.10.1; mechanised semantics exist in Isabelle (Jinja) and Leroy's verification survey.
level_notes.0: HotSpot in openjdk/jdk is the reference implementation (other JVMs: OpenJ9, GraalVM). There is no official textual assembly syntax; Jasmin, asmtools jasm and Krakatau define community assembler syntaxes, and javap prints a de-facto disassembly format.

languages.name: K
languages.summary: Rewrite-based executable semantic framework in which a programming language is defined by its syntax (BNF productions with attributes), a configuration of nested cells and rewrite rules; from one definition K derives a parser, interpreter, symbolic executor and a matching-logic deductive verifier. languages.name: Kahn process networks
languages.summary: Kahn's 1974 model of deterministic parallel computation: sequential processes communicating only through unbounded FIFO channels with blocking reads, whose semantics is the least fixed point of continuous functions on streams. level_notes.1: Kahn's 1974 IFIP paper is not openly online; the 1977 Kahn-MacQueen report is on HAL.
level_notes.0: Ptolemy II's process-network domain is the best-known executable implementation.

languages.name: Kotlin
languages.summary: Statically typed language from JetBrains targeting the JVM, JavaScript, WebAssembly and native code, with null-safe types, declaration-site variance, extension functions, data/sealed classes and compiler-supported coroutines. Its K2 compiler front end (FIR) feeds a shared IR used by all back ends.

level_notes.0: One implementation: JetBrains/kotlin (K2 front end = PSI parser + FIR; back ends for JVM bytecode, JS, Wasm and Kotlin/Native via LLVM share the 'IR' tree). The repository is too large for directory listings here, so links point at individual files on master. Coroutine library machinery lives in Kotlin/kotlinx.coroutines.
level_notes.1: No ISO/ECMA standard. The Kotlin language specification (kotlinlang.org/spec, source in Kotlin/kotlin-spec) is the normative description of Kotlin/Core; it lags the compiler, so KEEP proposals (Kotlin/KEEP, branch main, files named KEEP-nnnn-*.md) and the compiler define newer features.
level_notes.2: The official documentation at kotlinlang.org/docs is explanatory (guide/tour style) and is filed at level 2; only its keyword table and grammar reference are filed at level 1.

languages.name: KRC
languages.summary: Small lazy functional language by David Turner (University of Kent, 1979-81), a simplified SASL that introduced pattern-matching recursion equations and list comprehensions ('ZF expressions'); used for teaching at Kent and Oxford and a direct ancestor of Miranda.

level_notes.1: Turner's 'Recursion Equations as a Programming Language' (1981) is the defining paper; the krc(1) manual page and the 1981 prelude/library listings document the language.

languages.name: KornShell
languages.summary: Bourne-compatible shell from Bell Labs that added command-line editing, functions with local scope, arrays, associative arrays (ksh93), floating-point arithmetic, coprocesses and [[ ]] tests; ksh88 was the main basis of the POSIX shell standard.

level_notes.1: Defined by AT&T ksh88/ksh93 and their manual pages plus Bolsky & Korn's book; POSIX sh standardised a subset of ksh88. Public-domain clones (pdksh, OpenBSD ksh, MirBSD mksh) differ in details.
level_notes.0: ksh93/ksh is the maintained continuation (ksh 93u+m) of AT&T's ksh93 from att/ast; OpenBSD ksh and mksh are pdksh descendants.

languages.name: Untyped lambda calculus

level_notes.0: A theoretical model: level 0 lists mechanised metatheory (Isabelle, Coq, Agda/PLFA), the TAPL reference evaluators and well-known interpreters/universal machines rather than a canonical implementation.

level_notes.3: No Rosetta Code category; Wikipedia, nLab, PLDB and esolangs cover it.

languages.name: λμ-calculus
languages.summary: Parigot's extension of the lambda calculus with named terms and a μ binder that captures continuations, giving a Curry-Howard interpretation of classical natural deduction; variants include de Groote's unstratified syntax, call-by-value λμ and Curien-Herbelin's symmetric λμμ̃.

level_notes.0: No canonical implementation or widely used mechanisation; control operators appear in real languages as call/cc (Scheme) and shift/reset.
level_notes.1: Defined by Parigot (LPAR 1992); Griffin (POPL 1990) first typed call/cc classically; Curien & Herbelin (ICFP 2000) define λμμ̃.

languages.name: LaTeX
languages.summary: Document markup language and macro package built on TeX: authors describe logical structure (sections, environments, cross-references, floats) and document classes and packages turn it into typeset output. The current kernel is LaTeX2e (since 1994), maintained by the LaTeX Project, with the expl3 programming layer (LaTeX3) now loaded in the format.

level_notes.0: The definition is the kernel source itself: latex3/latex2e (base/*.dtx literate sources, built into latex.ltx) plus the expl3 kernel in latex3/latex3, run on a TeX engine (pdfTeX, XeTeX, LuaTeX; see the tex entry). The l3build regression suite (base/testfiles) is the de-facto conformance test. LaTeXML, plasTeX, LaTeX.js, Pandoc, KaTeX/MathJax and Tectonic are alternative (often partial) implementations or converters.
level_notes.1: There is no formal standard. Authoritative are Lamport's book (LaTeX: A Document Preparation System, paywalled), the LaTeX Project's guides (usrguide, clsguide, fntguide, lthooks-doc, interface3) and the documented sources (source2e). The LaTeX2e unofficial reference manual (latexref.xyz) is the most complete open reference and is used here for section-level deep links.
level_notes.2: learnlatex.org (by LaTeX Project members), the Wikibooks LaTeX book and Overleaf Learn are the main open tutorials; TUGboat/LaTeX Project papers cover design and history.
level_notes.3: Wikipedia, PLDB, CTAN and the TeX FAQ index the ecosystem.

level_notes.0: No dedicated implementations; general Turing-machine simulators (e.g. JFLAP) model LBAs by restricting the tape.
level_notes.1: Myhill's 1960 technical report introduced LBAs; Kuroda (1964) linked nondeterministic LBAs to context-sensitive grammars.

languages.name: LOOP / GOTO / WHILE programs (Meyer-Ritchie)
languages.summary: Meyer and Ritchie's minimal imperative language over natural-number registers (increment, zero, assignment, and LOOP x DO ... END with a bound fixed on entry). languages.name: LOTOS
languages.summary: ISO formal description technique for OSI protocols and distributed systems that combines a CCS/CSP-style process algebra (behaviour expressions with gates, parallel composition and hiding) with the ACT ONE algebraic abstract data type language. level_notes.1: ISO 8807:1989 (paywalled) defines syntax and formal (structured operational) semantics. Bolognesi and Brinksma's 1987 tutorial is the classic introduction.
level_notes.0: The CADP toolbox (INRIA, closed source but free for academia) contains the CAESAR and CAESAR.ADT compilers for LOTOS and the LNT-to-LOTOS translator; its manual pages are the most accessible practical reference.

languages.name: Markdown
languages.summary: Lightweight plain-text markup language converted to (X)HTML, designed by John Gruber with Aaron Swartz to be readable as-is. The original dialect is defined only informally by the Daring Fireball syntax page and the Markdown.pl reference implementation; its ambiguities led to many flavours and to CommonMark.

level_notes.0: Markdown.pl (Perl, 1.0.1 of 2004; 1.0.2b8 beta) is the reference implementation and in practice the definition. Ports that track its behaviour (PHP Markdown, Python-Markdown, Showdown, Discount, Redcarpet, kramdown, Parsedown) and later parsers (marked, markdown-it, md4c) are listed; the mdtest suite descends from Gruber's MarkdownTest.
level_notes.1: There is no formal specification: Gruber's syntax page is descriptive and leaves many cases undefined. RFC 7763/7764 register the text/markdown media type and variant names; PHP Markdown Extra and MultiMarkdown documents define the most influential early extensions. CommonMark, GFM and Pandoc Markdown have their own entries.
level_notes.2: The Markdown Guide is the main tutorial; Atwood's and MacFarlane's essays explain why the dialect fragmented.
level_notes.3: Babelmark compares implementations side by side.

languages.name: OCaml
languages.summary: Statically typed ML-family language from Inria with Hindley-Milner type inference, algebraic data types and pattern matching, a powerful module system (signatures, functors, first-class modules), a structural object system and, since OCaml 5, shared-memory parallelism (domains) and effect handlers. Compiles to bytecode and native code.

level_notes.0: The Inria distribution (ocaml/ocaml: ocamlc bytecode compiler, ocamlopt native compiler, C runtime) is the reference implementation and effectively the definition. js_of_ocaml, Melange and OxCaml reuse its front end; camlboot is an independent bootstrap interpreter.
level_notes.1: There is no standard or formal specification of full OCaml. Part II of 'The OCaml Manual' (the language reference, with BNF) is the authoritative prose description; language changes go through ocaml/RFCs and pull requests against the compiler. Formal semantics exist only for subsets (OCaml light) and for individual features (objects, modules, effects, the memory model).
level_notes.2: Part I of the official manual is a tutorial and is listed at level 2. Real World OCaml and the Cornell CS 3110 textbook are the main free books.

languages.name: OMG IDL (CORBA / DDS Interface Definition Language)
languages.summary: C++-like, language-neutral interface definition language from the Object Management Group: modules, interfaces with operations and attributes, exceptions, structs, unions, enums, sequences and typedefs, mapped to many programming languages. Originally part of CORBA, IDL 4.x is a standalone, building-block-structured spec also used by DDS (with XTypes annotations).

level_notes.1: OMG specifications are freely downloadable as PDF (no section anchors). IDL 4.x splits the language into 'building blocks' (core data types, interfaces, value types, CORBA-specific, components, annotations...). Language mappings (IDL4-to-C++/Java) and DDS-XTypes are separate OMG specs.
level_notes.0: IDL compilers ship with ORBs and DDS implementations: TAO's tao_idl (flex/bison front end), omniORB's omniidl, eProsima Fast-DDS-Gen (ANTLR grammar), OpenDDS's opendds_idl.

languages.name: OpenAPI Specification
languages.summary: Vendor-neutral, JSON/YAML-encoded interface description language for HTTP APIs: an OpenAPI description declares servers, paths, operations, parameters, request/response bodies and security schemes, using (since 3.1) full JSON Schema 2020-12 for data models.

level_notes.1: Defined by the OpenAPI Initiative (Linux Foundation) specification documents published at spec.openapis.org; the Markdown sources in OAI/OpenAPI-Specification are authoritative and the published JSON Schemas for each minor version are normative companions (non-authoritative for validation). Companion specs Arazzo (workflows) and Overlay (document transformation) are also OAI standards.
level_notes.0: No reference implementation. The OAI-published JSON Schemas validate OpenAPI documents; widely used parsers/validators are swagger-parser (Java), kin-openapi (Go), openapi-spec-validator (Python), Spectral (linting) and openapi-generator (code generation). oasdiff detects breaking changes between versions.
level_notes.2: learn.openapis.org is the official OAI tutorial site; swagger.io's 'OpenAPI Guide' is the long-standing vendor tutorial.

languages.name: OpenQASM
languages.summary: Imperative quantum assembly / circuit-description language originating at IBM: OpenQASM 2 describes gate-level circuits on qubit registers, while OpenQASM 3 adds classical control flow, typed classical data, subroutines, timing (duration/stretch/delay/box) and pulse-level calibrations via OpenPulse.

level_notes.1: The live specification at openqasm.com (maintained by the OpenQASM Technical Steering Committee, with versioned 3.0/3.1 snapshots and an ANTLR grammar) defines OpenQASM 3; OpenQASM 2 is defined by the 2017 arXiv paper. level_notes.0: The openqasm/openqasm repo holds the grammar and the reference Python AST/parser (openqasm3 package). Production parsers live in Qiskit (Rust qasm2/qasm3 crates), qe-qasm (C++) and many SDKs (Braket, pytket, etc.).

level_notes.1: No standard: Perl's perlre is the original definition and PCRE2's pcre2pattern/pcre2syntax man pages document the library dialect (pcre2compat lists the differences). Deep links use the man pages' named anchors where present.
level_notes.0: PCRE2 (C; interpretive backtracking matcher, alternative DFA matcher and an SLJIT-based JIT) and Perl's own regcomp.c/regexec.c.

languages.name: Perl
languages.summary: Dynamically typed scripting language created by Larry Wall for text processing and system administration, notable for sigils, context-sensitive evaluation (scalar vs list), built-in regular expressions, reference-counted memory and a package/bless-based object model; perl5 is both the reference implementation and the de facto definition.

level_notes.0: perl5 (github.com/Perl/perl5, branch blead) is the only complete implementation and defines the language ('only perl can parse Perl'): toke.c is a hand-written context-sensitive lexer driving the Bison grammar perly.y, op.c builds and peep.c optimizes the op tree, pp*.c hold the opcode bodies run by run.c, sv.c/av.c/hv.c/gv.c implement the value model and symbol tables, regcomp.c/regexec.c the regex engine. Perlito and cperl are partial alternatives.
level_notes.1: No standard or specification: the perldoc pages shipped with perl (perlsyn, perldata, perlop, perlsub, perlre, perlobj, perlfunc, perlvar) are the official reference, and the perlNNNdelta pages are the release notes. Language changes go through PPCs (Proposed Perl Changes), introduced in 2021.
level_notes.2: Programming Perl (the 'Camel book') is the classic designer-authored book but is paywalled; Modern Perl and Higher-Order Perl are free online.
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code reports 'blocked' to automated checkers; metacpan.org rejects automated clients.

languages.name: PHP
languages.summary: Dynamically typed, reference-counted scripting language originally designed for server-side web templating, with a class-based object model, runtime-enforced type declarations and an RFC-driven evolution process; the Zend Engine in php-src is the reference implementation.

level_notes.0: php-src is the reference implementation: the Zend Engine (Zend/) holds the re2c scanner, Bison grammar, AST compiler, opcode VM (zend_vm_def.h is the template from which the executor is generated), GC and object model; ext/ holds the standard library, ext/opcache the optimizer and JIT. HHVM (see hack), PeachPie (.NET), KPHP and JPHP are alternative implementations of PHP dialects.
level_notes.1: No formal standard. The PHP Language Specification (php/php-langspec, rendered at phplang.org) was written by Facebook/Rex Jaeschke for PHP 5.6/7.0 and is no longer kept current; the php.net Language Reference plus accepted RFCs (wiki.php.net/rfc) describe the current language, and php-src behaviour is definitive.
level_notes.2: No HOPL paper; the manual's History chapter is the main first-party history.
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code reports 'blocked' to automated checkers.

languages.name: π-calculus
languages.summary: Milner, Parrow and Walker's process calculus of mobile processes: concurrent processes communicate over channels whose names can themselves be sent, so the communication topology changes during computation. It extends CCS with name passing and restriction and can encode the lambda calculus.

level_notes.0: A theoretical model: level 0 lists mechanised metatheory (Isabelle AFP Pi_Calculus and Psi_Calculi), verification tools built on the calculus (Mobility Workbench, ProVerif for the applied pi-calculus, TyPiCal) and small interpreters; Pict is the classic programming language built on the asynchronous pi-calculus.
level_notes.1: Defined by Milner, Parrow and Walker, "A Calculus of Mobile Processes I/II" (1989 LFCS reports, 1992 Information and Computation). Variants (polyadic, asynchronous, applied) have their own defining papers.

languages.summary: Apple's embeddable configuration-as-code language built around amendable, late-bound objects with classes, type constraints and generators, rendering to JSON, YAML, plists and other formats.

languages.name: PL/I
languages.summary: IBM's large general-purpose language for System/360, meant to unify FORTRAN, COBOL and ALGOL use cases: block structure, records and pictures, pointers and based storage, ON-conditions for exception handling, multitasking, a macro preprocessor and extensive built-in functions. Used to write Multics.

level_notes.1: ANSI X3.53-1976 / ISO 6160 are paywalled; the technically identical ECMA-50 is freely downloadable from Ecma. IBM's language reference manuals (1965 specifications, PL/I (F), PL/I for MVS & VM) are the vendor definitions; current Enterprise PL/I documentation on ibm.com refuses automated clients and is not linked.
level_notes.0: Production compilers (IBM Enterprise PL/I, Micro Focus) are proprietary. Iron Spring PL/I is a modern compiler for Linux/OS2 whose runtime library is open source; the Multics PL/I compiler survives in the Multics source releases.

languages.name: PL/M
languages.summary: Gary Kildall's block-structured systems language for Intel microprocessors (8008/8080, later 8086/386), derived from PL/I and XPL: BYTE/ADDRESS (WORD) types, BASED variables, structures, a literal-substitution macro facility and interrupt procedures. Used to write CP/M and Intel's ISIS operating system.

level_notes.1: Defined by Intel's PL/M programming manuals (scans on bitsavers); no standard.
level_notes.2: No modern secondary literature beyond the Wikipedia history; the 1973 Intel guide (level 1) doubles as the original tutorial.
level_notes.0: Kildall's original PL/M compiler was written in FORTRAN 66 (source preserved on the unofficial CP/M site); Mark Ogden has ported it to C and reverse-engineered Intel's ISIS-II PL/M-80 compiler back into PL/M source.

languages.name: Plankalkül
languages.summary: Konrad Zuse's 1942-45 high-level notation for his Z-series computers, with hierarchical bit-based data types (arrays, tuples/records), assignment, guarded conditionals, iteration, assertions and subroutines in a two-dimensional notation; first published in 1948 and fully in 1972, and first implemented decades later.

level_notes.1: The only definition is Zuse's own 1945 manuscript (published 1972 as GMD Bericht 63, English translation GMD Bericht 106); no open scan of either is available, so the original notation is accessed via Bauer & Wössner (1972) and Knuth & Trabb Pardo (1976). Level 1 therefore has no linkable entry.
level_notes.0: Zuse never implemented it. Implementations: Hohmann (1975 dissertation, not available), FU Berlin compiler (Rojas et al., 2000; report record linked), and a 2025 Python interpreter on GitHub/PyPI using a linearized notation. Line anchors refer to the main branch.
level_notes.2: Secondary literature is mainly historical papers and student theses.

languages.name: POSIX Shell Command Language
languages.summary: The shell command language standardised by POSIX.2 (IEEE 1003.2-1992) and now in XCU Chapter 2 of POSIX.1/Single UNIX Specification; a codification of the Bourne shell plus KornShell features, implemented by dash, ash, yash, ksh, bash --posix and others.
standards: The Open Group Base Specifications Issue 8

level_notes.1: Normative text is XCU Chapter 2 (Shell Command Language) plus the sh, test, printf, read, getopts... utility pages and XBD chapters on regular expressions, environment variables and utility conventions; it is freely readable on pubs.opengroup.org (Issue 8 = POSIX.1-2024; Issue 7 2018 edition also linked). The informative rationale is XRAT C.2. The ISO version (ISO/IEC 9945) is paywalled. Austin Group bug reports serve as the proposal process.
level_notes.0: There is no reference implementation; dash (Debian/Ubuntu /bin/sh), BusyBox ash, FreeBSD sh (all Almquist-shell descendants), yash and Oils OSH aim at POSIX conformance. Smoosh is an executable formal semantics written in Lem; Morbig is a static POSIX shell parser. Oils' spec/ directory is a large cross-shell conformance suite.
level_notes.2: Most tutorials teach bash; the ones listed here are specifically about portable/POSIX sh.

languages.name: Protocol Buffers
designers: Google (Jeff Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, Kenton Varda et al.)
languages.summary: Google's language-neutral interface definition language and binary wire format for structured data: .proto files declare messages, enums, oneofs, maps and services, protoc generates code, and field numbers plus tag-length-value encoding give forward/backward-compatible schema evolution. Syntax versions proto2 and proto3 are being superseded by feature-based Editions (2023, 2024).

level_notes.1: No standards-body specification. The language specifications (proto2, proto3 and Edition 2023 grammars), the language guides, the Encoding guide and the ProtoJSON/text-format specs on protobuf.dev are normative in practice; descriptor.proto is the machine-readable schema of schemas. Editions design documents are kept in the protobuf repository.
level_notes.0: protoc (C++, protocolbuffers/protobuf) is the reference compiler; upb is the C kernel behind Python/Ruby/PHP. The repository's conformance/ directory is the official cross-language conformance suite. Independent implementations: protobuf-go, protocompile (Buf), prost (Rust), protobuf.js.

languages.name: Python
languages.summary: Dynamically typed, garbage-collected general-purpose language with indentation-based block structure, a large standard library and optional (gradual) type annotations; defined by the Python Language Reference and the PEP process, with CPython as the reference implementation.

level_notes.0: CPython (C) is the reference implementation: PEG grammar in Grammar/python.gram, compiler and bytecode interpreter in Python/, built-in types in Objects/; its InternalDocs/ directory documents the internals. level_notes.1: No ISO/ECMA standard. The Python Language Reference and Library Reference (docs.python.org) are normative together with accepted PEPs; the static type system has its own specification at typing.python.org. Where the reference is silent, CPython behaviour is the de facto definition.
level_notes.2: The official Tutorial and HOWTOs are level 2; there is no HOPL paper, so Guido van Rossum's 'History of Python' blog and the Design and History FAQ serve as history sources.

languages.name: QBE intermediate language
languages.summary: Small textual SSA intermediate language of the QBE compiler backend, designed as a minimal alternative to LLVM IR: a handful of base types (w, l, s, d), aggregate types for C ABI compatibility, data definitions and functions made of blocks with phi, arithmetic, memory, call and jump instructions.

level_notes.0: QBE itself (C, about 10k lines) is the only implementation; its source is browsable through cgit at c9x.me. Front ends emitting QBE IL include cproc (C11) and Hare.
level_notes.1: The IL reference document at c9x.me (with older versioned copies v1.0-v1.2) is the definition.

languages.name: Query By Example

level_notes.0: No open implementation source; QBE survives in IBM QMF and in GUI query designers.

languages.name: Quantum circuits
languages.summary: Standard model of quantum computation as sequences of unitary gates on qubit wires followed by measurement; universal gate sets and circuit complexity underlie OpenQASM, Quil and nearly all quantum languages.

level_notes.0: Theoretical model: level 0 lists simulators, rewriting tools and mechanisations rather than a canonical implementation. Qiskit, Cirq and TKET are the dominant circuit frameworks.
level_notes.1: Deutsch 1989 (paywalled, DOI) and Barenco et al. 1995 define gates and universality.

languages.name: Quantum lambda calculus
languages.summary: Family of lambda calculi extending functional computation with quantum data: van Tonder's untyped calculus (2003) and Selinger-Valiron's linearly typed calculus with classical control (2004), basis of languages such as Quipper and QWIRE.

level_notes.0: Theoretical model: level 0 lists simulators, rewriting tools and mechanisations rather than a canonical implementation. No canonical implementation; Quipper and QWIRE realise the ideas.

languages.name: Quint

languages.name: R
languages.summary: Dynamically typed, lazily evaluated, vector-oriented language and environment for statistical computing and graphics; an open-source dialect of S with Scheme-style lexical scoping, first-class environments and several object systems (S3, S4, reference classes).

level_notes.0: GNU R (developed in Subversion, mirrored at wch/r-source) is the reference implementation and the de-facto definition. Alternative implementations: FastR (GraalVM), Renjin (JVM), pqR, Ř/RIR (research JIT), webR (GNU R on WebAssembly).
level_notes.1: No standard or formal specification. The 'R Language Definition' manual is officially still a draft; together with R Internals, Writing R Extensions and the per-function help pages it is the primary description. There is no numbered proposal process: R Core decides, with discussion on R-devel and Bugzilla. The Core R semantics in Morandat et al. (ECOOP 2012) is the main formalisation.
level_notes.2: 'An Introduction to R' is the official tutorial; Advanced R is the standard deep treatment of the language itself.

languages.summary: Declarative, Datalog-inspired query language of the Open Policy Agent (CNCF) for writing policies over JSON-structured data: rules (complete, partial set/object, functions, defaults, else-chains) are defined by bodies of expressions with unification, references, comprehensions, negation, 'some'/'every' quantifiers and a large built-in library; evaluation is top-down.

level_notes.0: open-policy-agent/opa (Go) is the reference implementation (ast parser/compiler/type checker, topdown evaluator); Microsoft's Regorus is an independent Rust interpreter.
level_notes.3: No Wikipedia or PLDB article; the OPA Playground is the main interactive resource.

languages.name: Relational algebra
languages.summary: Relational algebra is Codd's procedural query formalism over relations: selection, projection, rename, union, difference, Cartesian product and join (plus division, outer joins, grouping/aggregation and transitive-closure extensions); it underlies SQL semantics and query optimisation and is equivalent in power to safe relational calculus (Codd's theorem).

level_notes.0: Theoretical model; level 0 lists RelaX, an educational relational-algebra evaluator with a published grammar.
level_notes.1: Codd's 1970 CACM paper and 1972 'Relational Completeness' paper are the defining papers (open copies on university servers).
level_notes.2: Textbook chapters and course notes.

languages.name: Relational calculus

level_notes.0: Theoretical model; no notable dedicated implementation (QUEL and QBE are its practical descendants).
level_notes.1: Codd's 1972 'Relational Completeness of Data Base Sublanguages' defines the calculus and the completeness criterion.

languages.name: RISC-V

languages.name: Rust MIR
languages.summary: Mid-level intermediate representation of rustc: a control-flow graph of basic blocks with statements and terminators over places and rvalues, fully typed and desugared, on which borrow checking (NLL), const evaluation, Miri interpretation and MIR optimisations run before lowering to LLVM, Cranelift or GCC.

level_notes.0: Defined by rustc's data structures (rustc_middle::mir::syntax); Miri is an interpreter for MIR that detects undefined behaviour, and MiniRust is a reference-interpreter-style specification of a MIR-like core language.
level_notes.1: No stable specification: RFC 1211 introduced MIR, RFC 2094 (NLL) defines borrow checking on it; the generated rustc API docs are the reference for its constructs. std::intrinsics::mir allows writing MIR directly (unstable, for tests).
level_notes.2: The rustc dev guide chapters are the main explanation.
