languages.name: Rust
languages.summary: Systems programming language that guarantees memory and data-race safety without a garbage collector through ownership, borrowing and lifetimes, combined with traits, algebraic data types, pattern matching and zero-cost abstractions.

level_notes.0: rustc (rust-lang/rust) is the reference implementation and de facto definition; it contains the compiler (compiler/), the standard library (library/) and the UI test suite (tests/ui). Alternative implementations: gccrs (GCC front end), mrustc (bootstrapping compiler without borrow checking), rustc_codegen_cranelift and rustc_codegen_gcc (alternative back ends); Miri is an interpreter for MIR that detects undefined behaviour.
level_notes.1: There is no ISO/ECMA standard. The Rust Reference is the official but explicitly incomplete and non-normative language reference; accepted RFCs define individual features; the Ferrocene Language Specification (FLS, adopted by the Rust project in 2025) is a specification written for compiler qualification. Formal models (RustBelt, Stacked/Tree Borrows, Oxide, MiniRust, a-mir-formality) cover parts of the language.
level_notes.2: The official book ('The Rust Programming Language'), Rust by Example and the Rustonomicon are tutorials/guides and therefore level 2; the rustc dev guide is the internals guide.

languages.name: Scala

level_notes.1: No external standard. Changes go through the Scala Improvement Process (SIPs). The DOT calculus papers give a machine-checked core.

languages.name: Schematron
languages.summary: Rule-based XML validation language: patterns contain rules whose XPath context selects nodes and whose assert/report elements state natural-language-documented XPath conditions; phases, abstract patterns, variables and diagnostics are supported, and reports are produced in SVRL. languages.name: Scheme

languages.name: Scribe (Reid)
languages.summary: Brian Reid's document specification language and compiler (CMU, 1976-80, later sold by Unilogic): authors mark up text with @-commands naming logical environments (@section, @begin(quotation)...@end(quotation)) while separately written document-format definitions decide presentation. languages.name: SEQUEL / SQUARE (historic)
languages.summary: SQUARE (1973-75) and SEQUEL (1974), renamed SQL, were the IBM San Jose query languages designed by Chamberlin and Boyce for System R: SQUARE used a mathematical mapping notation, SEQUEL recast it as English keyword block structure (SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE), and SEQUEL 2 (1976) became the basis of SQL.

languages.name: Session types
languages.summary: Type disciplines for communication protocols: a channel's type describes the sequence of sends, receives and choices it must follow, ensuring protocol fidelity and (in many systems) deadlock freedom. level_notes.0: Many library and language embeddings exist (Rust, Haskell, Scala, OCaml, Links); one example library is listed.

languages.name: Setext

level_notes.1: The original bsdi.com setext documents (Feldman's "setext sermons", setext_concepts) survive only in archives and in the Docutils mirror (docutils.sourceforge.io, which blocks automated checks).

languages.name: SETL
languages.summary: Very-high-level language from NYU's Courant Institute built on finite sets, maps and tuples with set formers and quantifiers; used for executable specifications (Ada/Ed) and a direct ancestor of ABC and Python.

level_notes.0: GNU SETL (David Bacon) is the maintained implementation; historical CIMS SETL (LITTLE-based) and SETL2 sources are preserved at softwarepreservation.org. SetlX and ISETL are dialect interpreters.

level_notes.2: Most historical tutorials, papers and theses are scanned at the Computer History Museum Software Preservation Group site.

languages.name: SGML
languages.summary: A meta-language for defining markup languages: a document type definition (DTD) declares elements, attributes, entities and content models, and an SGML declaration fixes the concrete syntax (delimiters, tag minimisation). Descended from IBM GML; the parent of HTML (up to 4.01) and of XML, which is a simplified profile.

level_notes.0: James Clark's SP (and its successor OpenSP, hosted on SourceForge which blocks automated clients) is the standard parser; real DTDs such as HTML 4.01's are listed as machine-readable grammars.
level_notes.1: ISO 8879 is paywalled and no free draft exists; Goldfarb's SGML Handbook contains the annotated full text. ISO, ACM and w3.org links may show as blocked.
level_notes.2: The HTML 4.01 chapter "On SGML and HTML" is the most accessible free tutorial.

languages.name: Simply typed lambda calculus
languages.summary: The lambda calculus restricted by simple (arrow) types, introduced by Church in 1940 as the simple theory of types; it is strongly normalising (hence not Turing-complete), corresponds to intuitionistic propositional logic via Curry-Howard, and is the base case of nearly every typed functional language and type-soundness proof.

level_notes.0: Theoretical calculus: level 0 lists mechanised definitions and soundness/normalisation proofs (Software Foundations/Coq, PLFA/Agda, Isabelle, Metalib) and the TAPL reference type checkers.
level_notes.1: Church's 1940 JSL paper defines the simple theory of types; Curry (for the Curry-style variant), Tait (1967, normalisation) and Howard (1969/1980, formulae-as-types) are the other primary sources.

languages.name: Smalltalk (ANSI, Smalltalk-80, Pharo, Squeak)
languages.summary: Pure object-oriented, reflective language from Xerox PARC in which everything is an object and all computation is message sending, including control structures built from blocks. Smalltalk-80 defined the language, class library and bytecode virtual machine together; ANSI INCITS 319-1998 standardised the core, and Squeak, Pharo, GNU Smalltalk and commercial dialects carry it on.

level_notes.0: Squeak and Pharo descend from the Apple Smalltalk-80 image; their shared VM is OpenSmalltalk (Cog/Spur), generated from Smalltalk (VMMaker) to C. Pharo source is kept as Tonel .st files.
level_notes.1: The Blue Book (Goldberg & Robson 1983) defines Smalltalk-80 including a formal VM specification (Part Four); ANSI INCITS 319-1998 standardises the language core and protocols (paywalled; only unofficial drafts circulate). Blue Book deep links are PDF page links into the Ducasse free-books scan.
level_notes.2: Squeak and Pharo books (Pharo by Example etc.) are free.

languages.name: SMT-LIB
languages.summary: The common input and command language of satisfiability-modulo-theories (SMT) solvers: an S-expression syntax for many-sorted first-order formulas over standardised background theories (integers, reals, bit-vectors, arrays, floating point, strings, datatypes) plus a script language (declare-fun, assert, check-sat, get-model, push/pop) with an operational semantics for interacting with solvers.

level_notes.1: Defined by the SMT-LIB Standard reference document (Barrett, Fontaine, Tinelli; v2.7 of 2025, v2.6 still the most widely implemented), plus the separate machine-readable theory and logic declarations on smt-lib.org. Section links use #page=N into the PDF (PDF page = printed page + 1). Solver manuals (cvc5, Z3) document non-standard theories (sequences, sets, bags, finite fields).
level_notes.0: No single reference implementation: Z3, cvc5, Yices 2, Bitwuzla, MathSAT and OpenSMT each implement their own SMT-LIB parser; Dolmen is a standalone parser/typechecker that tracks the standard closely.
level_notes.3: No PLDB entry was found for SMT-LIB.

languages.name: SNOBOL4 / SPITBOL
languages.summary: Bell Labs string-processing language family (SNOBOL 1962 to SNOBOL4 1967) whose statements are subject/pattern/replacement lines with success/failure gotos; patterns are first-class values with backtracking that exceed regular expressions, and SPITBOL is its fast compiled implementation.

level_notes.0: SNOBOL4 was implemented in the SIL macro language ('The Macro Implementation of SNOBOL4'); CSNOBOL4 (Phil Budne) is a C build of that SIL code, and SPITBOL (now spitbol/x64 on GitHub) is an independent, much faster compiler written in the MINIMAL machine-independent assembly language.
level_notes.1: No ANSI/ISO standard; 'The SNOBOL4 Programming Language' (2nd ed., 1971, the 'Green Book') is the definition, preceded by the 1964 JACM paper on SNOBOL.
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code reports 'blocked' to automated checkers.

languages.name: Solidity

level_notes.0: solc (C++) in ethereum/solidity (now hosted under argotorg) is the reference compiler with a legacy codegen and a Yul-IR (via-IR) pipeline; Solang is an independent LLVM-based compiler.

languages.name: PostgreSQL SQL dialect
languages.summary: The SQL dialect of PostgreSQL: a highly standard-conforming, extensible SQL with user-defined types, operators, index access methods and procedural languages, rich built-in types (arrays, ranges, JSONB), CTEs, window functions, MVCC transactions with serializable snapshot isolation, and descent from Berkeley POSTGRES/PostQUEL.
standards: ISO/IEC 9075:2023 (core conformance target; see Appendix D of the manual)

level_notes.0: One implementation defines the dialect: postgres/postgres (parser in src/backend/parser with the Bison grammar gram.y, planner in src/backend/optimizer, executor in src/backend/executor). Level 0 also lists independent re-implementations and extractions of the dialect's grammar (libpg_query, CockroachDB's sql.y, ANTLR, sqlglot, sqlfluff, sqlparser-rs).
level_notes.1: The PostgreSQL manual (Part II 'The SQL Language' and Part VI 'Reference') is the normative description of the dialect; ISO/IEC 9075 is paywalled, so the ISO catalogue page, Appendix D (conformance) and free BNF extractions are linked. The Berkeley POSTGRES design papers are the defining papers of the system's data model and rule/extension design.
level_notes.2: The official tutorial (Part I) and the manual's Internals part are filed here, with books and courses on internals.
level_notes.3: Encyclopedia and catalogue pages; Rosetta Code only has a generic SQL category.

languages.name: SQLite SQL dialect
languages.summary: The SQL dialect of the embedded SQLite library: a large subset of standard SQL with dynamic (per-value) typing, type affinity, a single-file database format and a bytecode virtual machine (VDBE) that every statement is compiled to.

level_notes.0: The canonical source lives in a Fossil repository at sqlite.org/src; github.com/sqlite/sqlite is the official read-only mirror linked here. The parser is generated by Lemon from src/parse.y; every statement is compiled to VDBE bytecode executed by src/vdbe.c.
level_notes.1: There is no specification separate from the implementation: the 'SQL As Understood By SQLite' pages on sqlite.org (with railroad syntax diagrams), the file-format document and the C-API reference are the normative description, and the test suites (TCL tests, sqllogictest, proprietary TH3) are the conformance evidence.
level_notes.2: sqlite.org itself publishes much of the best explanatory material (query planner, atomic commit, architecture); these are listed as level 2 guides/internals guides.

languages.name: SQL (ISO/IEC 9075)
languages.summary: The standard relational database language: a declarative query, data-definition and data-manipulation language standardised as ISO/IEC 9075 (SQL-86 through SQL:2023), derived from IBM's SEQUEL and grounded in Codd's relational model, implemented in many vendor dialects.

level_notes.0: No reference implementation exists. Level 0 lists independent parsers and grammars written against the standard text (Jake Wheat's simple-sql-parser, the H2/Calcite/ZetaSQL-style parsers) and the sqllogictest corpus.
level_notes.1: ISO/IEC 9075 is paywalled; ISO catalogue pages are linked for each part, and the freely published BNF grammars (Ron Savage, Jake Wheat) derived from the standard text stand in for the syntax. Wikipedia's SQL:20xx pages summarise each revision.
level_notes.2: Modern SQL (Markus Winand) is the main free source of standard-SQL feature explanations with conformance tables; Use The Index, Luke covers indexes. Founding papers (Codd 1970, Chamberlin & Boyce 1974) are listed as original papers.

languages.name: Standard ML

level_notes.0: Several independent, conforming implementations exist: MLton (whole-program optimising), SML/NJ (interactive, incremental), Poly/ML, MLKit (region-based memory), Moscow ML, HaMLet (a direct transcription of the Definition) and the verified CakeML dialect.
level_notes.1: The language is defined by The Definition of Standard ML (Revised) (Milner, Tofte, Harper, MacQueen; MIT Press 1997), a formal natural-semantics specification; the SML family site hosts open PDFs with the publisher's permission. The Definition is a single PDF without stable section anchors, so concept deep links at level 1 point to the SML Basis Library pages instead.
level_notes.3: Wikipedia and PLDB cover SML; Rosetta Code reports 'blocked' from the research sandbox.

languages.name: Swift Intermediate Language (SIL)
languages.summary: High-level SSA intermediate language of the Swift compiler, sitting between the type-checked AST and LLVM IR; it keeps Swift semantics (generics, protocols, ownership, enums, closures) explicit so that mandatory diagnostics (definite initialisation, exclusivity) and high-level optimisations run on it. It has a textual form usable in tests.

level_notes.0: Implemented only in the Swift compiler (swiftlang/swift): SILGen produces SIL from the AST, SILOptimizer transforms it, IRGen lowers it to LLVM IR; parts of the optimizer are written in Swift (SwiftCompilerSources).
level_notes.1: The docs/SIL/*.md documents in the compiler repository are the official, evolving reference; there is no stable or versioned specification.
level_notes.3: No dedicated Wikipedia article; covered within the Swift article.

languages.name: Swift

level_notes.0: The Swift compiler (swiftlang/swift: C++ front end, SIL optimizer, LLVM-based IRGen) plus its standard library and runtime written in Swift/C++ is the reference implementation. swift-syntax is a second, Swift-written parser used by macros and tooling; Foundation, SwiftPM and SourceKit-LSP live in sibling repositories.
level_notes.1: No ISO/ECMA standard. 'The Swift Programming Language' (TSPL) Language Reference with its grammar summary is the normative-in-practice reference; accepted Swift Evolution proposals define individual features. docs.swift.org (DocC) renders section ids with JavaScript, so #fragments on TSPL pages were verified against the DocC JSON data rather than the static HTML.
level_notes.2: TSPL's Language Guide part is a tutorial (level 2). Slava Pestov's 'Compiling Swift Generics' and the compiler's docs/ folder are internals guides.

languages.name: System F
languages.summary: The polymorphic (second-order) typed lambda calculus, discovered independently by Girard (1971/72, as a proof system for second-order arithmetic) and Reynolds (1974, for parametric polymorphism). It adds type abstraction and application to the simply typed lambda calculus; it is strongly normalising, its type inference is undecidable, and it underlies GHC Core, ML polymorphism and the theory of parametricity.

level_notes.0: Theoretical calculus - level 0 lists reference type checkers (Pierce's TAPL fullpoly), mechanised metatheory (Coq/Autosubst, Agda) and production compilers whose core language is an extension of System F (GHC Core / System FC).
level_notes.1: Defined by Girard's 1971/72 work and Reynolds' 1974 paper; several publisher links are paywalled and report 'blocked'. Girard's thesis is linked from his own site.

languages.name: SystemVerilog
designers: Accellera (Co-Design Automation SUPERLOG donation, Synopsys Vera/OpenVera donation)
languages.summary: Hardware design and verification language standardised as IEEE 1800 (2005, 2009, 2012, 2017, 2023); a superset of Verilog adding rich data types, interfaces, packages, a class-based object system with constrained randomisation, functional coverage and SystemVerilog Assertions. Since 2009 IEEE 1800 subsumes IEEE 1364 Verilog.

level_notes.1: IEEE 1800 is the normative definition; the standard is paywalled but IEEE 1800 (and 1800.2 UVM) is free of charge through the IEEE GET Program (registration). No open working draft is linked; implementation manuals (Verilator, slang, Yosys) are filed at level 2 as they document tool support, not the language.
level_notes.0: No reference implementation. Open implementations: Verilator (compiled simulator), slang (complete front end/elaborator), Surelog/UHDM (parser with ANTLR grammar), Verible (parser/linter), sv2v (SV-to-Verilog converter), Yosys (synthesisable subset), CIRCT Moore dialect; the sv-tests suite measures conformance across tools.
level_notes.2: Free tutorials (ChipVerify, ASIC World, Doulos, Verification Guide) and many freely downloadable conference papers (Sutherland, Cummings); the main books (Sutherland et al., Spear & Tumbush) are commercial.

languages.name: TLA+ / PlusCal
languages.summary: Leslie Lamport's specification language that combines Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory with the Temporal Logic of Actions to describe concurrent and distributed systems as state machines; PlusCal is an algorithm language that translates to TLA+. level_notes.1: No ISO/industry standard. PlusCal is defined by Lamport's two PlusCal manuals.
level_notes.0: SANY (parser/semantic analyser), TLC (explicit-state model checker), the PlusCal translator and TLATeX live in tlaplus/tlaplus (Java). Apalache (symbolic, SMT-based model checker, Scala) and TLAPS/tlapm (proof manager, OCaml) are independent implementations of large parts of the language.
level_notes.2: Book section links use #page=N into the free PDFs (PDF page numbers, not printed page numbers).

languages.name: TOML
languages.summary: Minimal configuration file format designed to map unambiguously to a hash table: INI-like [tables] and dotted keys, typed scalars (strings, integers, floats, booleans, first-class RFC 3339 date-times), arrays and inline tables. Used by Cargo, pyproject.toml, Hugo and many other tools.

level_notes.1: The versioned specification at toml.io (v1.1.0 current, v1.0.0 widely implemented) is normative, with an ABNF grammar (toml.abnf) kept in the toml-lang/toml repository alongside the in-development spec text and changelog. There is no standards-body version; the MIME type application/toml was registered with IANA.
level_notes.0: No reference implementation: toml-lang/toml-test is the official language-agnostic conformance suite (valid/invalid cases with JSON expected output for decoders and encoders). Level 0 samples many independent parsers (CPython tomllib/tomli, BurntSushi/toml, go-toml, toml-rs, toml++, toml11, tomlkit, smol-toml, Tomlyn, tomlj).

languages.name: TraceQL
languages.summary: Query language of Grafana Tempo for distributed traces: spanset filters over span intrinsics and attributes ({ span.http.status_code >= 500 }), combined with logical and structural operators (parent/child, ancestor/descendant, sibling), piped through aggregators, grouping and selection, plus TraceQL metrics functions producing time series.

level_notes.1: Defined by the Tempo documentation (TraceQL pages, sourced from docs/sources/tempo/traceql in the repo) and the goyacc grammar in pkg/traceql; the 2022 design proposal records the intended semantics. The rendered docs carry no static section anchors.

languages.name: Typed Assembly Language (TAL)
languages.summary: Family of assembly languages with static type annotations (code types for labels, polymorphism, existential types, stack and alias types) whose type system guarantees memory and control-flow safety of machine code; introduced by compiling System F to a RISC-like TAL in a type-preserving compiler, and realised for IA-32 as TALx86 in the Cornell TALC project.

level_notes.0: The TALC releases (Cornell, up to 3.0) contain the TALx86 assembler/type checker and the Popcorn compiler, distributed as zip archives.
level_notes.1: Defined by the research papers (POPL 1998 / TOPLAS 1999 and follow-ups on stack-based TAL, modular linking, alias types), which give formal semantics and type-soundness proofs.

languages.name: TypeScript
languages.summary: A statically checked, structurally and gradually typed superset of JavaScript from Microsoft whose types are erased at compile time; the compiler (tsc) type-checks and emits plain ECMAScript.
standards: ECMA-262 (runtime semantics of the JavaScript it erases to)

level_notes.0: Two official implementations: the original self-hosted compiler written in TypeScript (src/compiler on the release-6.0 branch of microsoft/TypeScript, the last JavaScript-based line) and the native Go port that became TypeScript 7 (microsoft/typescript-go). swc, esbuild, Babel and oxc only parse and strip types; they do not type-check.
level_notes.1: There is no maintained specification: the TypeScript Language Specification was last updated for TypeScript 1.8 (2016) and is archived in the repository. Current behaviour is defined by the compiler, per-release notes, the design goals/notes in the TypeScript wiki and, for runtime semantics, ECMA-262.
level_notes.2: The TypeScript Handbook is official but explanatory (it explicitly is not a specification), so it is filed at level 2.
level_notes.3: Rosetta Code reports 'blocked' to automated checkers.

level_notes.0: The OCaml reference interpreter in WebAssembly/spec (interpreter/) accompanies the spec and runs the official .wast conformance suite in test/core; SpecTec (spectec/) now generates the spec's formal rules. Independent implementations: wabt (C++ tools and interpreter), Binaryen (optimizer IR), wasmtime/Cranelift and wasm-tools (Rust), WAMR and wasm3 (interpreters), V8 Liftoff/TurboFan, SpiderMonkey, JavaScriptCore.
level_notes.1: Normative: the W3C Core Specification (living draft at webassembly.github.io/spec, versions 1.0/2.0 as W3C Recommendations, 3.0 released 2025), plus the JS API and Web API specs. Features enter through the phased proposals process; proposal overview documents are linked here. The core spec contains a full formal semantics and soundness theorem; mechanised versions exist (WasmCert-Isabelle, WasmCert-Coq).
level_notes.2: MDN's WebAssembly guides and instruction reference, the PLDI 2017 design paper by the designers (listed as level 1 original-paper), performance studies and blog posts on engine internals.

languages.name: Web IDL

languages.name: x86 / x86-64 assembly
designers: Intel (8086 ISA: Stephen Morse et al.)
languages.summary: Family of assembly languages for the Intel x86 instruction set architecture and its 64-bit AMD64/Intel 64 extension, written in Intel syntax (MASM, NASM, YASM, FASM) or AT&T syntax (GNU as); each assembler adds its own directives, macro system and expression language on top of the vendor-defined instruction set.
standards: Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual

level_notes.1: The instruction set is defined by vendor manuals (Intel SDM, AMD APM; no independent standard). Each assembler's manual defines its syntax and directives (NASM manual, GNU as manual, Microsoft MASM reference). Calling conventions are defined by the System V psABI documents (x86-64 and i386) and Microsoft's x64 conventions. x86-TSO is the accepted formal memory model.
level_notes.2: Felix Cloutier's HTML extraction of the SDM instruction reference is listed at level 2 as a derived guide; tutorials and university guides cover both syntaxes.
level_notes.3: Wikipedia, PLDB and Rosetta Code (Rosetta reports blocked from the sandbox).

languages.name: XDR (RFC 4506)

level_notes.1: RFC 4506 (STD 67) defines both the encoding and the XDR language (Section 6); it supersedes RFC 1832 and RFC 1014. RFC 5531 (ONC RPC) extends the language with program/version/procedure definitions.
level_notes.0: The original Sun RPC code survives in glibc/libtirpc (xdr.c primitives) and the rpcgen compiler; other implementations include Python's former xdrlib and Go's go-xdr.
level_notes.2: Secondary literature is mostly ONC RPC / rpcgen programming guides in vendor manuals; the Python library reference is the closest maintained tutorial-style text.

languages.name: XML
typing: schema-typed (DTD attribute types, external schema languages)
languages.summary: A simplified profile of SGML standardised by the W3C: a Unicode text syntax for labelled trees of elements, attributes and character data, with entities, DTD validation, and a family of companion specifications (Namespaces, Infoset, XInclude, xml:id, canonicalization). The substrate of XHTML, SVG, SOAP, office formats and countless configuration and interchange vocabularies.

level_notes.0: No reference implementation exists; conformance is defined by the W3C/NIST/OASIS XML Conformance Test Suite. The dominant parsers are linked: libxml2 and Expat (C), Xerces (Java/C++, also inside the JDK), plus the standard-library parsers of Python, Go, .NET and several Rust/JS/OCaml implementations that differ in which optional features (DTD, external entities, namespaces) they implement.
level_notes.1: XML 1.0 Fifth Edition is the normative core; it embeds the DTD language (catalogued separately as `dtd`). www.w3.org answers this catalog's link checker with HTTP 403 (reported `blocked`); every W3C anchor below was verified by fetching the page with a different client. Namespaces, Infoset, XML Base, xml:id, XInclude and Canonical XML are separate Recommendations layered on the core; XSD, RELAX NG, XPath, XSLT and XQuery have their own catalog entries.
level_notes.2: Secondary literature is vast but much of the classic material (IBM developerWorks, Sun, Cover Pages) has moved or vanished; surviving canonical items (Bray's Annotated XML, Harold's books, TEI's Gentle Introduction, platform parser guides, security cheat sheets) are linked.
level_notes.3: Wikipedia has separate articles for most sub-topics (namespaces, DTD, CDATA, entity attacks), linked individually because they are section-level tertiary sources.

languages.name: XQuery
languages.summary: W3C-standardised functional query language over the XQuery and XPath Data Model (XML nodes, atomic values, and since 3.1 maps and arrays/JSON); a superset of XPath with FLWOR expressions, node constructors, modules and higher-order functions. Recommendations 1.0 (2007), 3.0 (2014), 3.1 (2017); 4.0 is drafted by the QT4 Community Group.

level_notes.1: Defined by a family of W3C Recommendations: XQuery 3.1 (language), XPath and XQuery Functions and Operators 3.1, the XQuery and XPath Data Model 3.1, Serialization 3.1, and the (1.0-only) Formal Semantics. www.w3.org returns a Cloudflare 403 to the link checker; all w3.org anchors were verified with a plain curl fetch. XQuery 4.0 drafts live at qt4cg.org.
level_notes.0: No single reference implementation; conformance is measured with the W3C QT3 test suite (qt3tests, and qt4tests for 4.0). BaseX (Java), Saxon (Java/C#; Saxon-HE is open source, its repository mainly ships releases), eXist-db (ANTLR grammar), Zorba (C++, dormant) and Galax (OCaml, historical) are representative implementations.
level_notes.2: Books: Walmsley's 'XQuery' (O'Reilly); Wadler's typed-functional XQuery tutorial; the Wikibooks XQuery cookbook.

languages.name: YAML
languages.summary: Human-oriented data serialization language with indentation-based block structure, a JSON-compatible flow syntax, anchors/aliases for shared and cyclic nodes, and tags resolved through schemas. Ubiquitous as a configuration format.

level_notes.0: There is no single reference implementation. libyaml (C, YAML 1.1) underlies PyYAML, Psych and many bindings; yaml-reference-parser is generated mechanically from the 1.2 spec productions; yaml-test-suite is the shared conformance corpus that implementations are compared against (matrix.yaml.info).
level_notes.1: The YAML 1.2.2 specification (yaml.org) is normative; many deployed parsers still implement YAML 1.1 with its larger implicit-typing rules, so the 1.1 spec and the 1.1 type repository are linked as well. RFC 9512 registers the media type.
level_notes.2: Much secondary literature is implementation- or tool-specific (PyYAML, Ansible, Kubernetes/Helm); critical essays on implicit typing are included because they explain the 1.1/1.2 differences.

languages.name: Z notation
languages.summary: Model-based formal specification notation from the Oxford Programming Research Group, built on typed Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory and first-order predicate logic, with schemas and a schema calculus for structuring specifications of states and operations. Standardised as ISO/IEC 13568:2002.

level_notes.1: ISO/IEC 13568:2002 defines syntax, type system and semantics; it is one of ISO's publicly available standards (free zip download). Before that, Spivey's Z Reference Manual (ZRM, 2nd ed. 1992), now freely distributed by the author, was the de-facto standard and is still the dialect most tools and textbooks use. Section links point into the ZRM PDF served from the author's GitHub repository via jsDelivr (#page=N is the PDF page).
level_notes.0: There is no reference implementation: fuzz (Spivey; type checker for the ZRM dialect, C) and the Community Z Tools (CZT; Java, parser/type checker/animator for ISO Z and Object-Z) are the main open implementations. Z is usually written as LaTeX markup (zed/fuzz style files) or in Unicode/ZML.

languages.name: Zig
languages.summary: Low-level systems language positioned as a modern replacement for C: no hidden control flow or hidden allocations, explicit allocators, error unions with try/catch/errdefer, optionals instead of null pointers, and compile-time execution (comptime) used for generics and reflection. The zig toolchain doubles as a C/C++ cross compiler.

level_notes.0: The self-hosted compiler (Zig, with LLVM, C and native x86-64/aarch64/wasm/... backends) is the reference implementation. Development moved from GitHub to Codeberg (codeberg.org/ziglang/zig) in late 2025; github.com/ziglang/zig is the archived former home. Codeberg serves anti-scraper pages to automated clients, so the Codeberg file links were verified against the repository tree from the Codeberg API rather than by the link checker. Pipeline: tokenizer -> Parse (AST) -> AstGen (ZIR) -> Sema (AIR, comptime evaluation) -> codegen/link.
level_notes.1: No standard and no complete formal specification: the Language Reference (one HTML page per release, linked here for 0.17.1) is the de-facto definition together with the compiler; the zig-spec repository holds an unfinished draft spec and the PEG grammar. Language changes are proposals filed as issues in the issue tracker; release notes document each language change. Zig is pre-1.0 and breaks compatibility between minor releases.

languages.name: Zot
languages.summary: Chris Barker's 2002 extension of Jot with input/output via continuation-passing style.

level_notes.1: No separate author specification could be verified; the encyclopedia/wiki entry describes the language.

languages.name: ZPL
languages.summary: Implicitly parallel array language from the University of Washington: computations are expressed over regions (index sets) with direction offsets, and the compiler derives the communication and a WYSIWYG performance model for distributed-memory machines; a precursor of Chapel domains.

level_notes.0: Compiler distributions are linked from the UW project page; no maintained repository.
level_notes.1: The ZPL Programmer Guide and Chamberlain thesis are distributed via the UW site.

languages.name: Z shell (zsh)
languages.summary: Bourne-compatible interactive shell and scripting language with ksh and csh features, powerful globbing (qualifiers, recursive **), parameter-expansion flags, associative arrays, loadable modules and a programmable completion system; the default login shell on macOS since 2019.

level_notes.1: No specification; the Zsh manual (zsh.sourceforge.io, which blocks automated access here, so section links point to the identical Debian zshmisc/zshexpn/zshparam man pages) documents the implementation. Yodl sources of the manual live in Doc/Zsh in the repository.
level_notes.0: The C implementation (zsh-users/zsh, mirror of the SourceForge git repo) is the definition; Test/*.ztst is its regression suite.

general.title: Side-by-side language references and multi-language code collections
general.description: Sites and documents that show the same construct, idiom or program in many languages at once: Learn X in Y Minutes, Programming-Idioms (with individual idioms mapped to concepts), Pascal Rigaux's "Syntax across languages" (per-construct anchors and per-language columns), the Wikipedia "Comparison of programming languages" family (per-section anchors), 99 Bottles of Beer, the Hello World Collection, PLEAC, Sample Programs, Exercism tracks and Wikibooks cross-language books. Rosetta Code and Hyperpolyglot have their own collections (rosetta-code-tasks, hyperpolyglot). Every "languages" list was derived from the site's own language index and mapped to catalog ids; languages without a catalog id are omitted.

resources.title: Learn X in Y Minutes — index of language tours
resources.notes: One-page annotated code tours (a single commented source file per language/tool), all following the same pattern: comments, primitives, variables, collections, control flow, functions, modules, classes. Per-language pages live at https://learnxinyminutes.com/<slug>/; the language list here covers the pages that map to catalog ids.

resources.title: adambard/learnxinyminutes-docs — Markdown sources of the Learn X in Y Minutes tours
resources.notes: Markdown sources (one file per language plus translations); useful to see all tours side by side or diff them.

resources.title: Programming-Idioms — the same small task in many languages
resources.notes: ~370 idioms, each with a one-line specification and one or more implementations per language (Python, Java, Go, Rust, C++, C#, JS, Pascal, Haskell, Fortran, Ada, COBOL ...). Pascal entries are mostly Free Pascal/Delphi; "VB" is Visual Basic .NET; "Lisp" is Common Lisp.

resources.notes: Matrix showing which idioms have an implementation in which language.

resources.notes: Any language pair can be requested as /cheatsheet/<Lang1>/<Lang2>; a single language as /cheatsheet/<Lang>.

general.title: Wikipedia cross-language comparison pages
general.description: English Wikipedia's cross-language comparison material: the 'Comparison of programming languages' family (general, syntax, basic instructions, strings, string functions, list comprehension, object-oriented programming, algebraic data types, associative arrays, arrays, type systems, multi-paradigm and functional languages), comparisons of data-serialization formats, document and lightweight markup languages, relational DBMSs, regex engines, parser generators, assemblers, shells, ISAs, VMs, template engines and documentation generators; pairwise comparisons (C# vs Java, Java vs C++, C# vs VB.NET, VB vs VB.NET, Pascal vs C, Pascal vs Delphi, C vs C++ compatibility); the per-language example sections of concept articles (exception-handling syntax, higher-order functions, string interpolation, coroutines, generators, iterators, async/await, null-coalescing and safe-navigation operators, here documents, entry points, option types, tagged unions, enumerations, reflection, mixins, generics, ...); and the language lists and timelines (by type, by generation, timeline, history, JVM/CLI, concurrent, educational, compilers). Every section anchor was checked against the rendered page's heading ids. `languages` lists the catalog ids of languages whose own Wikipedia article is linked from that table/section (or whose sub-section it is), so it is a lower bound for very large tables.

general.description: English Wikipedia articles that give language-independent background for each concept id in data/concepts.json: the canonical article for the concept first, then closely related articles (named idioms, classic problems, algorithms, theory). Entries are ordered by the taxonomy; the first concept tag of an entry is its primary concept. A few articles are about one language's realisation of a concept (e.g. 'Generics in Java'); those carry a `languages` list. Section anchors were verified against the rendered page. Cross-language comparison tables live in wikipedia-comparisons.json.
